snippet.title: The Arizal on Datan and Aviram's Tikkun Through Eliyahu | Part 6 | Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltVDgCK2hQ6DpURicujUN6s

In part 6, the conclusion of this 6-part English Torah series on Datan, Aviram, and Korach, Rabbi Eliyahu Bari turns to the Arizal’s astonishing teaching: the story of Datan and Aviram does not simply end when the earth swallows them in the rebellion of Korach.

According to the Arizal, their spiritual root appears later in the story of Eliyahu HaNavi at Har Carmel, one of the greatest public revelations of Hashem in Tanach. This final class shows how even the distorted force that opposed Moshe can eventually be redirected into Kiddush Hashem.

The Arizal places Korach, Datan, and Aviram in shoresh Kayin, the spiritual root of Kayin. This root is connected with powerful Gevurah, enormous spiritual force, and real danger when that force is not sweetened. That already changes the way we understand them. They are not random troublemakers. They are spiritually charged souls whose power becomes destructive when it is detached from humility, Shalom, and submission to Hashem.

In Sefer HaLikutim on Parashat Korach, the Arizal connects Datan and Aviram to the two bulls of Eliyahu at Har Carmel. One bull is chosen for Hashem, and the other is chosen for Baal. The Arizal explains that Datan was more sweetened, while Aviram was harsher. Yet even the bull assigned to Baal ultimately becomes part of the revelation of Hashem’s Name.

That is the depth of the tikkun. In the Korach story, Datan and Aviram stand against Moshe and become part of machloket. In the Eliyahu story, their root is forced back into Kiddush Hashem. Even the side that externally appears connected to Baal becomes part of the declaration: Hashem Hu HaElokim.

This does not mean Datan and Aviram were secretly right. They were not. The Torah condemns their rebellion. But the Arizal teaches us not to flatten them into simple villains. Their force was real. Their potential was real. Their corruption was real. And their eventual tikkun is real.

The final lesson of the series is that holy potential must be sweetened. Gevurah without humility becomes accusation. Pain without submission becomes machloket. Spiritual power without Shalom becomes rebellion. But when that same force is brought back to Hashem, it can become part of Kiddush Hashem.

1. In this video:
1. The Arizal’s teaching that Datan and Aviram belong to shoresh Kayin.
2. Why Korach, Datan, and Aviram share a powerful Gevurah root.
3. The two bulls of Eliyahu at Har Carmel and their connection to Datan and Aviram.
4. Why Datan is described as more sweetened and Aviram as harsher.
5. How even the bull connected to Baal becomes part of Kiddush Hashem.
6. Why this tikkun does not justify the rebellion, but deepens our understanding of it.
7. The final life lesson: questions, pain, and spiritual force must be sweetened by humility, Shalom, and service of Hashem.

2. Main sources discussed:
1. Shaar HaGilgulim, Hakdamah 36.
2. Sefer HaLikutim, Parashat Korach.
3. The story of Eliyahu HaNavi at Har Carmel.
4. The declaration “Hashem Hu HaElokim.”
5. The broader connection between Gevurah, machloket, tikkun, and Kiddush Hashem.

snippet.title: Ramad Vali | Why Moshe’s Life Ended in Vengeance: Mystical Secrets Unveiled - Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IlvwX-VzvbP2OAVnAQj46u0B

Why did Moshe Rabbeinu’s life both begin and end with vengeance? Why was this act — taking revenge against Midian — the final mission Hashem commanded him to complete before death? In this powerful shiur, Rabbi Eliyahu Bari explores the deeply mystical teachings of the Ramad Vali, revealing the spiritual truths hidden within Parshas Matos and the war against Midian. This is more than a story of retribution — it's a profound look into Divine justice, kedusha, and the soul’s journey.

The Ramad Vali, a towering Kabbalist and commentator, explains that Moshe's life started with a courageous act of self-sacrifice — defending a fellow Jew from an Egyptian oppressor — and was destined to conclude with an even more spiritually significant act: avenging Hashem’s honor through a sacred war. This symmetry was not coincidental but divinely orchestrated.

Why did the Torah emphasize choosing “men” for this battle? Why was it necessary to enlist 1,000 from each tribe, even including the tribe of Levi which normally does not engage in war? The answer lies in the spiritual mission of the battle. The soldiers selected were not merely warriors — they were exalted men, infused with holiness, handpicked for their spiritual stature. Only such men, intimately connected to the Shechina, could be vessels for Hashem’s vengeance.

And yet, they were only 12,000 against an entire nation. What gave them victory? According to the Ramad Vali, these warriors “gave over” their entire beings, aligning themselves so completely with Hashem’s will that they were shielded by the Source of Life Himself — and not a single soldier died. Their success wasn’t military — it was metaphysical.

What of the Midianite women — weren’t they the ones who led Bnei Yisroel astray? Yes, but the Ramad Vali explains the deeper dynamic: the men of Midian forced the women to participate. Women of marital age were not spared, but the core blame was placed on the male orchestrators and their leaders — the kings and Bilaam himself.

Bilaam's death is perhaps the most mysterious. Why does the Torah say he was killed by sword? Isn’t “killed” always assumed to be by sword? The Ramad Vali reveals that Bilaam, filled with sorcery, believed himself immune to physical weapons — protected by amulets and magic. But Pinchas, wielding the sword of kedusha, shattered that illusion. The battle wasn’t between men — it was between forces of light and darkness.

Even more fascinating is that Pinchas refused to use Hashem’s Name to kill Bilaam. He only used the Divine Name to find Bilaam, hidden in mid-air through sorcery. To kill him with Hashem’s Name would have conferred a spark of holiness — something Bilaam, steeped in impurity, could not merit. Instead, he was slain by kedusha made manifest in a sword — the same weapon Bilaam mocked.

This video is a spiritual journey into the heart of Divine vengeance — not vengeance fueled by anger, but by justice, truth, and sanctity. It’s about leaders who serve not themselves but the mission of Hashem. It’s about war that is truly holy, conducted only by those worthy of carrying the Divine Presence within them.

Rabbi Eliyahu Bari delivers this lesson with depth, clarity, and reverence for the teachings of the Ramad Vali. Perfect for those seeking not just to learn the parsha but to penetrate its hidden dimensions. If you're looking to grow in your Torah learning, your appreciation of Chumash, or your connection to the mystical path of the Ramad Vali, this shiur is essential.

snippet.title: Ramad Vali - Devarim - Fighting the Seven Levels of Tumah in the Desert - Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IlvwX-VzvbP2OAVnAQj46u0B

Why does Sefer Devarim open with a list of locations from Bnei Yisrael’s desert journey? According to Kisvei Ramad Vali, these places represent much more than geographical markers — they reflect a deep, mystical structure of tumah (impurity) and the challenge of maintaining kedushah (holiness) in a spiritually barren world.

This video explores how each location Moshe mentions at the beginning of Devarim alludes to sins that Bnei Yisrael committed — each connected to one of the seven levels of tumah. Instead of conquering these impure forces, the nation often fell into their trap. As Moshe approached his final days, he sought not just to rebuke, but to repair — to re-instill holiness and to spiritually cleanse the camp before Yehoshua would take over.

Ramad Vali explains that this transition from Moshe to Yehoshua marked a cosmic shift from the “sun” (male) to the “moon” (female) aspect of kedushah. The sun shines its own light — a symbol of direct Divine guidance — whereas the moon reflects light, making it more susceptible to spiritual infiltration. It’s a dynamic that mirrors the male and female spiritual energies: active force vs. receptive vessel.

Knowing the danger of this shift, Moshe expounded and repeated the Torah — not only to rebuke, but to fortify. The very first word: “Devarim” (Words) alludes to the feminine aspect now being elevated. The phrase “asher diber Moshe” (“which Moshe spoke”) has initials that spell “Adam”, representing the 45-value male element that integrates into and uplifts the female.

Ramad Vali shows how Moshe's final mission was to align the masculine and feminine aspects of kedushah, to safeguard Bnei Yisrael from falling prey to tumah as they prepared to enter Eretz Yisrael. This teaching speaks directly to our generation: how do we maintain spiritual strength when the guidance feels indirect? How can we reinforce kedushah when leadership and energy change form?

How does Ramad Vali explain the transition from Moshe to Yehoshua?

snippet.title: Ramad Vali – Chayei Sarah – Did Sarah Fix the Sin of Chava? – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete English series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IlsqrZV4iVEQjZAqDuYTHHVs

Why does the Torah describe Sarah's life with such specific detail — one hundred years, twenty years, and seven years? And why is her age recorded at all, unlike other women in the Torah? In this class, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the mystical insights of Ramad Vali and uncovers the spiritual purpose behind Sarah’s 127 years of life.

According to Ramad Vali, Sarah’s “life” truly began only after the birth of Yitzchak. Before that, her years of barrenness were not considered years of “living.” Just like Rachel, who said, “Give me children or I am dead,” the essence of womanhood in Torah thought is deeply connected to motherhood and spiritual productivity.

The gematria of the word “Vayehi” (ויהיו) is 36, and when adding the kolel (the unity of the word), it equals 37 — the age of Yitzchak at the time of the Akeidah. The Torah begins with “Vayehi chayei Sarah” — hinting that her life essentially ended when she heard about the binding of Yitzchak. Her soul could not withstand even the idea of his slaughter and departed immediately.

Ramad Vali goes even deeper: the 127 years of Sarah’s life correspond to 126 streams of Gevurah (Divine Judgment) which she rectified. These streams are rooted in the five letters of the Divine Name Elokim, which has 5 letters and therefore 120 permutations (5 factorial = 120), spread across six directions — east, west, north, south, up, and down — totaling 126.

Sarah, in her righteousness, repaired the destructive version of Gevurah introduced into the world by Chava through Cain — the first expression of corrupted judgment and violence. In contrast, Sarah gave birth to Yitzchak — the refined expression of Gevurah, pure and elevated.

After she completed this monumental spiritual mission, she passed away in the 127th year — her mission on Earth completed.

--- IN THIS VIDEO ---

Why are Sarah’s years listed in three segments — 100, 20, and 7?

What does the gematria of “Vayehi” tell us about the end of Sarah’s life?

Why are the barren years of her life not counted?

How did Sarah spiritually repair what Chava damaged through Cain?

What are the 126 streams of Gevurah and how do they relate to her age?

This deep class reveals the immense spiritual power of Sarah Imeinu, and the cosmic mission embedded in the years of her life. It gives us a new perspective on life, purpose, motherhood, and rectification.

snippet.title: Ramad Vali – Chayei Sarah – The Secret of the Cave of Machpela – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete English series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IlsqrZV4iVEQjZAqDuYTHHVs

What was so special about the Cave of Machpela that Avraham insisted on purchasing it in full, and in private? In this class, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the deep mystical meaning behind Maaras HaMachpela as revealed by Ramad Vali.

After the death of Sarah, Avraham turns to the people of Cheis and calls himself both “a stranger and a resident.” Ramad Vali explains that he was truly a stranger — but now, with Sarah buried there, part of him had become a permanent resident. The soul is connected to where the body is buried, and Avraham knew he would one day be buried there as well.

Avraham urgently sought to bury Sarah without delay, to prevent impure spiritual forces from attaching to her holy body. While the people of Cheis wanted her buried among them, Avraham refused — he did not want Sarah to be exposed to the spiritual contamination of the wicked. He insisted on a separate place, protected and pure.

That place was Maaras HaMachpela — the "double cave." On a surface level, it’s called “doubled” because of its two tiers. But Ramad Vali explains its mystical meaning: the cave represents the gateway to Gan Eden, and it mirrors the two letters hei (ה) in the Divine Name. These represent two spiritual gates — the upper and lower “hei” — which righteous souls pass through upon leaving this world.

Avraham intentionally concealed the cave's spiritual power by referring to it merely as “the edge of the field.” Had the people of Cheis understood its holiness, they would have denied him access. Ephron, unaware of its depth, saw no divine light and readily agreed to sell.

The pasuk in Yeshayahu (26:2) says: “Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter” — in plural — hinting to these two gates of holiness that Avraham saw.

The name "Machpela" can also be read as “Hei–Machpela” — the doubled ‘hei’ — referencing the Divine Name, and hinting at the cave's function as a portal between worlds.

--- IN THIS VIDEO ---

Why does Avraham call himself both a stranger and a resident?

What spiritual danger was Avraham trying to avoid by burying Sarah quickly?

Why was the Cave of Machpela called “doubled”?

What are the two gates of holiness, and how are they connected to the Divine Name?

How did Avraham see spiritual light in the cave that no one else could see?

This class will open your eyes to the deep spiritual architecture of the Torah’s most famous burial site, and how Avraham’s foresight secured more than just land — he secured a doorway to eternity.

snippet.title: Ramchal - Toldot - Chesed and Gevurah: Why Yitzchak Re-Dug Avraham’s Wells - Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:

Why did Yitzchak re-dig the wells of his father Avraham? What is the spiritual meaning behind this seemingly simple act? In this profound teaching, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the Kabbalistic commentary of Ramad Vali (from Otzros Ramchal) on Parshat Toldot and reveals how these three wells symbolize the very foundation of the Jewish people. 

The Torah tells us that Yitzchak dug the same wells of water his father once dug. But why repeat the same action? The Ramchal teaches us that every act of the Avos had deep spiritual impact — they were building the infrastructure for future generations, repairing the spiritual worlds with every step. 

✔ What does water represent in Kabbalah and why is it connected to Avraham? 
✔ Why did the Plishtim stop up the wells after Avraham’s death? 
✔ How does Yitzchak's attribute of gevurah work to amplify his father’s chesed? 
✔ Why did conflict arise after the first two wells but not the third? 
✔ What does the third well reveal about Yaakov and the future of Klal Yisrael? 

The first well symbolizes Avraham and his son Yishmael — from whom impurity emerged. The second well stands for Yitzchak and Esav — another source of spiritual distortion. Only the third well, representing Yaakov and his all-righteous descendants, is free of conflict, showing that when purity is unbroken, tumah has no hold. 

Through this lesson, we learn that Yitzchak didn’t merely continue his father’s mission — he elevated it. By digging the wells anew, he infused them with gevurah, properly balanced with chesed, creating a perfected spiritual channel. And by calling the wells by the same names, he honored the exact tikkunim of his father while strengthening them for future generations. 

When he completed this mission, Hashem blessed him because of Avraham My servant — teaching us that when we uphold the legacy of our ancestors, we become worthy of their blessings.

Why Yaakov’s purity made the third well untouchable by tumah 

How the synthesis of chesed and gevurah brings Divine blessing 

Join Rav Eliyahu Bari as he uncovers the hidden wisdom behind the Three Wells of Kindness — a lesson not just in history, but in building spiritual foundations for the future.

snippet.title: Ramad Vali - Toldot - The Deeper Meaning of “The Elder Shall Serve the Younger” - Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:

What did Hashem mean when He told Rivka, “Two nations are in your womb”? What is the inner spiritual message behind “the elder shall serve the younger”? In this powerful lesson, Rav Eliyahu Bari reveals the deep Kabbalistic insights of Ramchal (Ramad Vali) on Parshat Toldot — and how the physical body reflects this divine prophecy. 

In this class, we explore the mystical view of Yaakov and Esav as more than just historical figures — they symbolize two eternal forces battling through history. Drawing from the Ramchal's writings, Esav represents the liver, the seat of anger and ego, while Yaakov embodies the heart, the seat of understanding and humility. 

✔ What is the true meaning of “the elder shall serve the younger” (ורב יעבד צעיר)? 

✔ Why does the placement of the liver and heart in the body hint at their spiritual roles? 

✔ How does Esav’s declaration “I have plenty” expose his ego versus Yaakov’s humility? 

✔ What does it mean that kings will one day lick the dust of Israel’s feet? 

✔ How does this prophecy reflect the ultimate spiritual destiny of the Jewish people? 

Through this lens, the struggle of Yaakov and Esav is not just one of power, but of spiritual orientation: the haughty will one day serve the humble. Just as the liver is physically larger but must serve the heart, so too will Esav — who glorified himself as "rav" (great) — serve Yaakov, who diminished himself before God. 

Ramchal explains that during exile, even when it seems Israel is suppressed, the spiritual structure of the world remains unchanged: the nations are meant to assist and elevate Israel. This relationship will reach its true fulfillment in the time of Redemption when, as prophesied in Isaiah 49:23, “Kings will be your nurturers… and the dust of your feet they will lick.” 

This isn’t about dominance, but about recognition: the nations of the world will yearn to partake in the holiness of Israel — even its dust will hold more value to them than their former power.

snippet.title: The Secret Connection Between Yosef and Chanukah Revealed - Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Yosef and Chanukah—two radiant sources of light in the darkest times. In this deep, original shiur (lesson), Rav Eliyahu Bari uncovers powerful parallels between Yosef's destiny and the miracle of Chanukah, drawing from Kabbalah, Midrash, Chassidut, and Gematria. Through the lens of inner Torah, we explore how Yosef’s spiritual power became the key to overcoming Greek darkness—and how his light continues to shine through the flames of the Chanukiah. 

Yosef is not just a biblical figure. He represents the ideal Tzaddik—the guardian of the covenant who brings holiness even into exile. Chanukah is not merely a commemoration; it’s a yearly reawakening of the Hidden Light capable of transforming both individuals and nations. Their convergence in the calendar is no accident—it’s a profound spiritual message. 

From this shiur, you will discover: 

Why the names "Yosef" and "Antiochus" share the same numerical value (Gematria 156), revealing the inner spiritual battle of the Chanukah era. 

How Yosef became a divine channel of light in Egypt, associated with the Sefirah of Yesod—the conduit of spiritual energy connected to the start of Chanukah. 

Why the Greeks banned circumcision and how this act aimed to sever the flow of divine influence—making the Maccabean victory a restoration of that sacred channel. 

How the mystical interpretation of Yosef’s coat (ketonet passim) hints at two "garment festivals"—Chanukah and Purim, both celebrating hidden miracles. 

Why the debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on candle lighting reflects Yosef’s mission: spreading light even to those considered "unworthy." 

How a Tzaddik’s inner work can ignite light in others—and why Chanukah calls on us to go beyond ourselves and shine outward. 

 

--- IN THIS VIDEO --- 

How the Gematria of Yosef reveals his mission against Antiochus 

Why Yosef embodies the Sefirah of Yesod—linked to 25 Kislev 

How Yosef represents sanctified service despite exile 

How Chanukah light heals Yosef’s family rift and brings unity 

Why the oil miracle and Yosef’s essence both symbolize hidden holiness defeating natural law 

This shiur dives deep into the spiritual anatomy of Chanukah: why it lasts eight days, spans two months (Kislev and Tevet), why its flames cannot be used for personal gain—and how all this ties back to Yosef. 

We explore teachings from the Arizal on the Yesod-Chanukah connection, Zohar’s insights on Yosef’s role in history, perspectives from the Chatam Sofer, and modern voices from Breslov and Chabad. Each element builds a sacred structure of light—not just surviving darkness, but transforming it. 

Chanukah is not a memory. It’s a mission. It’s a moment when each of us can become like Yosef—guarding our inner light through betrayal, exile, or challenge. Yosef didn’t just forgive his brothers—he added light to their lives. Likewise, when we light the menorah, we are called to bring light to those around us. 

Watch till the end to awaken that same light within you—the light of Yosef, the light of Torah, the light of an eternal covenant that can never be extinguished.

snippet.title: Or HaChaim – Va’era – Why the Patriarchs Did Not See What Moshe Saw – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3Ilv9NkvH-GFUhdlP0utnmeuP

Why does the Almighty, having already established a covenant with the Patriarchs, nevertheless reveal Himself to Moshe on a fundamentally different level? And why does the redemption from Egypt not occur immediately, despite a clear Divine promise? In this profound lesson on Parashat Va’era, one of the most subtle explanations of the Or HaChaim’s commentary is revealed, addressing the nature of covenant, revelation, and Divine mercy. 

Rabbi Rav Eliyahu Bari carefully analyzes the words of the verse “וגם הקימותי את בריתי – ‘And I also upheld My covenant,’” explaining that even if the Almighty had fully fulfilled His covenant with the Patriarchs, the level of revelation granted to Moshe would still have remained unique. The Patriarchs knew the Almighty as El Shaddai, but the full revelation of the Divine Name Hashem is directly connected to the process of the Geulah and to Moshe’s mission. 

The Or HaChaim emphasizes that the Almighty was “obligated” to the Patriarchs not only with revelation, but also with the realization of His oath — the redemption of their descendants from slavery. Yet even when the time for fulfillment arrived, the redemption did not take place instantly. Why? Because the Almighty activated the attribute of mercy — middat ha-rachamim. He knew that Moshe would face Pharaoh’s stubbornness, the despair of the people, the sea ahead and the Egyptian army behind. Without internal preparation, Moshe might not have been able to withstand the emotional and spiritual burden. 

This is the central idea of the lesson: Geulah is not merely an exit from Egypt. It is a prolonged process whose ultimate goal is the conquest of the Land of Israel and the transformation of the nation into a bearer of the Divine Presence. Even the delay of redemption becomes part of the Almighty’s merciful plan. 

Special attention is given to the words “את ארץ מגוריהם” — “the land of their sojourning.” Why does the Torah not simply say “the land of Canaan”? The Or HaChaim explains that the status of being “strangers” began already in the time of the Patriarchs, and this is what counts toward the four hundred years of exile that were foretold to Avraham. Moreover, the double use of the word “את” hints at the inclusion of additional territories, such as the land of the Philistines, expanding our understanding of the Promised Land and the historical process of the Geulah. 

This lesson uniquely combines textual precision, philosophical depth, and a practical approach to faith, patience, and Divine guidance throughout history.

snippet.title: Or HaChaim – Bo – Two Types of Darkness in Egypt – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3Ilv9NkvH-GFUhdlP0utnmeuP

Why does the Torah describe Moses stretching out his hand to bring the plague of darkness, when every other plague is associated with the use of the staff? Why does the Torah change its language specifically at this stage of the Exodus? This class explores a deep and precise insight of Or HaChaim that reveals the true nature of the final plagues in Egypt.

In this lesson, Rav Eliyahu Bari analyzes Or HaChaim’s commentary on Parashat Bo, focusing on a striking deviation in the Torah’s description of the plagues. In the immediately preceding plague of locusts, God commands Moses to stretch out his hand, yet the Torah still records that Moses used his staff. Throughout the plagues, the staff is consistently the instrument through which divine punishment is carried out. However, when the Torah describes the plague of darkness, it suddenly states: “Moses stretched forth his hand toward the heavens.” This change demands explanation.

Or HaChaim explains that this shift reflects a fundamental transformation in the nature of the plagues themselves. Drawing on Midrash Shemot Rabbah, he teaches that the darkness of Egypt was not ordinary darkness. It was the darkness described in Psalms as divine concealment—“He made darkness His hiding place.” This darkness was not the absence of light but a spiritual reality, an entity that originated beyond the natural world.

Because this darkness was supernatural, Moses understood that it would be inappropriate to confront it in the same way as earlier plagues. The staff represents authority and action within the created order. It is effective when nature itself is being struck. But when the plague originates above nature, from a realm of divine concealment, the staff is no longer the proper instrument. Out of reverence and spiritual sensitivity, Moses did not raise his staff upward. Instead, he stretched out his hand alone.

The Midrash records an additional opinion: that the darkness came from Gehinnom. Or HaChaim explains that this view does not contradict the first. In fact, both can be true. There were two distinct types of darkness in Egypt. One lasted three days during which the Egyptians could not see one another but were still able to move. The second lasted an additional three days during which they were completely immobilized, unable to rise from their places.

These were not merely physical conditions but stages of judgment. One removed perception; the other removed agency. Together, they demonstrate that Egypt was not only being punished but spiritually dismantled. The final plagues were no longer disruptions of nature but revelations of divine power that transcended the natural order entirely.

Rav Eliyahu Bari emphasizes that this insight reshapes our understanding of the Exodus. The plagues were not simply escalating in severity; they were escalating in spiritual intensity. Moses’ change in action reflects his awareness that human tools—even prophetic ones—have limits. When the challenge is spiritual rather than natural, restraint and reverence are themselves forms of service.

This lesson offers a timeless message. There are moments when familiar methods no longer work, not because they are weak, but because the situation requires a different level of response. Or HaChaim teaches us how to recognize the difference between natural struggle and spiritual confrontation, and how humility before God becomes the greatest strength.

snippet.title: Or HaChaim – Bo – The Secret of “All the Israelites Had Light” – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3Ilv9NkvH-GFUhdlP0utnmeuP

How could the Israelites experience light while standing in the very homes where Egyptians were trapped in total darkness? Why does the Torah emphasize the words “and for all the Israelites there was light”, and what deeper truth is hidden in this unusual phrasing? This class reveals a profound teaching of Or HaChaim about the nature of light, darkness, and spiritual perception.

In this lesson, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores Or HaChaim’s explanation of the plague of darkness in Parashat Bo, focusing on a subtle but critical detail in the Torah’s wording. The Torah does not merely say that the Israelites had light. It says “and for every Israelite there was light.” Or HaChaim explains that this teaches something extraordinary: whenever a Jew entered the home of an Egyptian, he experienced light even there, in the very place where the Egyptian remained trapped in darkness.

Or HaChaim offers an even deeper interpretation. Where did this light come from? The answer is startling. The light originated within the homes of the Egyptians themselves. The same environment, the same space, and the same reality produced two opposite experiences. For the Egyptians, it was darkness. For the Israelites, it was light.

This leads to a radical conclusion: the darkness of Egypt was not purely objective. It was subjective, tied to the spiritual condition of the person experiencing it. The sages teach that the wicked “wrap themselves in darkness,” while the righteous are able to access light even in places of concealment. Or HaChaim explains that this is why the Torah adds the phrase “in their dwellings”—to indicate that nothing external changed. Only the inner reality of the observer did.

The plague of darkness, then, was not merely a punishment. It was a revelation. It exposed the inner state of Egyptian society, which had become spiritually corrupt and disconnected from divine truth. At the same time, it revealed the elevated spiritual state of the Israelites, who were already living in a reality of light even before their physical redemption.

Rav Eliyahu Bari emphasizes that this idea is essential to understanding the Exodus. Redemption begins internally. Long before the Israelites left Egypt geographically, they had already exited Egypt spiritually. Their ability to perceive light where others perceived darkness was proof that they were ready for freedom.

This teaching carries a powerful message for all generations. Two people can stand in the same situation, face the same challenges, and yet experience completely different realities. Or HaChaim teaches that light and darkness are not only external conditions but reflections of one’s spiritual orientation. When a person aligns with truth, faith, and purpose, light emerges even in the darkest places.

snippet.title: Or HaChaim – Bo – Why Israel Took Egypt’s Wealth – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3Ilv9NkvH-GFUhdlP0utnmeuP

Why does the Torah emphasize that the Israelites acted “according to the word of Moses” when taking silver, gold, and vessels from Egypt? Why is it necessary to clarify their motivation, and what deeper lesson is being taught about prophecy, obedience, and reward? This class reveals a subtle but powerful teaching of Or HaChaim about faith under moral tension.

In this lesson, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores Or HaChaim’s explanation of the Israelites “borrowing” valuables from the Egyptians before the Exodus. At first glance, this episode appears troubling. The Israelites asked for items under the assumption that they would soon return them, yet they left Egypt permanently. Or HaChaim insists that the Torah goes out of its way to explain that this was not motivated by greed or desire for wealth.

The key phrase is “they did according to the word of Moses.” The Israelites did not initiate this request. They were uncomfortable with it. Their natural moral instinct resisted creating a misleading impression. However, Moses was a fully authenticated prophet of God, and his instruction carried divine authority. Because the command was temporary and tied to an emergency moment of redemption, the people were obligated to comply.

Or HaChaim connects this episode to a fundamental principle articulated by Maimonides: when a true prophet issues a temporary command that appears to contradict standard Torah law, the people must obey—provided the instruction does not involve idol worship. This was precisely such a case. The Israelites followed Moses not because it felt right, but because obedience to divine prophecy demanded it.

The Torah then states that the Egyptians “lent” them these items and that Israel “emptied Egypt.” Or HaChaim explains that the subject of this sentence is often misunderstood. It was not the Israelites who aggressively took wealth. Rather, God granted them favor in the eyes of the Egyptians, and the Egyptians themselves pressed valuables upon them, even against the will of the Israelites.

This detail proves something remarkable: at that moment, the Israelites were not even thinking about permanent departure or material gain. Their entire focus was freedom. Had they been motivated by greed, they would have demanded far more. Instead, their lack of interest in wealth became the very reason they received it in abundance.

Rav Eliyahu Bari emphasizes that this teaching overturns conventional assumptions. Wealth came not through desire, but through restraint. Not through calculation, but through faith. The Egyptians “emptied themselves” because God intervened on behalf of a people whose priorities were aligned with redemption, not profit.

The Talmud teaches that the Israelites were so consumed with the vision of leaving Egypt that material possessions held no appeal for them. As a reward for this elevated mindset, God ensured they left with great wealth anyway—miraculously and without moral compromise.

This lesson speaks powerfully to every generation. When a person acts מתוך אמונה—out of faith and obedience rather than self-interest—blessing arrives from unexpected directions. Or HaChaim teaches that true reward follows spiritual integrity, not pursuit.

snippet.title: Can You CHEAT the Manna System? Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IlsKP1OQ374qdZMGDIqXtwEs

🔥 COULD YOU CHEAT GOD'S MANNA SYSTEM? 🔥

For 40 years in the wilderness, our ancestors lived on manna—a food that defied all known laws of nature, economics, and physics. Each person was allocated exactly one omer per day. But here's an intriguing question: What if someone tried to cheat the system? Could you eat manna right there in the field while gathering, then still bring home your full omer?

In this class, we deeply investigate this question through the lens of the great Torah commentators.

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS:
00:00 - Introduction: A Puzzle in the Wilderness
05:30 - How the Miracle Worked: The Equalization
12:15 - Rashi: The Miracle of Volume
16:40 - Malbim: The Satiety Factor
21:00 - Netziv: The Personalized Omer
25:20 - Halachic Analysis: Is This Stealing?
32:45 - The Biology of Manna: Why You Physically Couldn't Cheat
38:10 - Gemara Yoma 75a: Food With No Waste
43:30 - The Wicked vs. The Righteous
48:00 - "Nothing Over" - The Final Seal
53:15 - The Shabbat Exception Proves the Rule
57:40 - Conclusion: Why the Loophole Is Impossible

📚 FOUR TYPES OF IMPOSSIBILITY:

1️⃣ METAPHYSICAL: The omer measured your soul's capacity for that day. (Rashi, Malbim) The miracle was retroactive—stomach content + basket content = always exactly 1 omer.

2️⃣ BIOLOGICAL: Manna was "lechem abirim"—absorbed completely, NO WASTE (Yoma 75a). Your body was like a vessel; once full with one omer, no more could fit.

3️⃣ LEGAL/SPIRITUAL: Not "poel" (worker's lunch)—this was bread from heaven with specific divine terms. (Brisker Rav) The omer defined manna's very existence for you. Eating unmeasured = "gezel" (theft) from Hashem—you'd get calories but miss spiritual nourishment.

4️⃣ LOGISTICAL: For the faithless, manna was hard coriander seeds requiring grinding, pounding, boiling. The sun heats up and manna melts (Exodus 16:21). The righteous found ready-to-eat bread at their doorstep.

🎯 KEY CONCEPTS:
• Bitachon (absolute trust in Divine providence)
• The equalization miracle
• Lechem min hashamayim (bread from heaven)
• Divine justice and economics
• Spiritual food vs. physical food
• Da'at (knowledge) as a metaphor for manna

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS TODAY:
Manna teaches us that Hashem provides exactly what we need, when we need it, in the way we need it. Our job is to trust the system, not try to outsmart it. In the face of Divine Providence, there are no loopholes.

snippet.title: Black Hole Cosmology & Tzimtzum 1/4 – Intro – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IluxxOqJUCNHI-Vj3V6VpciE

What if modern astrophysics is rediscovering what Kabbalah described centuries ago? Could spinning black holes and the cosmic axis of the universe reflect the mystical doctrine of Tzimtzum — the Divine contraction that made creation possible?

In this profound and thought-provoking lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the fascinating parallels between rotating black holes, cosmic spin, and the Lurianic concept of Tzimtzum as taught by Rabbi Isaac Luria, the Arizal. Modern physics suggests that our universe may exist inside a spinning black hole, inheriting a preferred axis of rotation from a “parent universe.” Meanwhile, Kabbalah teaches that before creation, the Infinite Light (Ohr Ein Sof) filled all reality until a Divine contraction concealed that light, forming a metaphysical void where creation could unfold.

Astrophysical discoveries — including surprising evidence that galaxies may share a common rotational direction — challenge the assumption of a random universe. If the cosmos has a preferred axis, what does that imply? Physicist Nikodem Popławski’s black hole cosmology proposes that every black hole could generate a new expanding universe beyond its event horizon. In this model, gravitational collapse becomes a cosmic womb, and rotation becomes inherited structure.

Remarkably, this scientific narrative echoes the Kabbalistic structure of Tzimtzum. First, contraction and concealment. snippet.title: Black Holes and Kabbalah: The Arizal’s Tzimtzum and Modern Cosmology
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IluxxOqJUCNHI-Vj3V6VpciE

Did our universe begin inside a spinning black hole? 

Modern astrophysics is exploring a bold possibility: that our universe may have been born inside a rotating black hole in a larger cosmos. At the same time, the Arizal (Rabbi Isaac Luria) teaches that creation began with Tzimtzum — a Divine concealment of Infinite Light, followed by a measured re-entry of light into a hidden space. 

Are these two ideas connected? 

In this lecture, we explore the structural parallels between black hole cosmology and the Kabbalistic concept of Tzimtzum. This is not an attempt to force Torah into physics or physics into Torah. Rather, it is a comparison of patterns — contraction, concealment, emergence, and structure. 

Recent astronomical observations have suggested something surprising: many galaxies appear to rotate in the same direction. If confirmed, this challenges the idea that the universe is completely random and isotropic. Some physicists, including Nikodem Popławski, argue that if the universe has an overall spin, it may have inherited that rotation from something larger — possibly a spinning black hole in a “parent” universe. 

In black hole cosmology, a massive star collapses into a black hole. Instead of ending in a final singularity, some models propose that the collapse “bounces” and expands from within, appearing as a Big Bang from the inside. In that case, every black hole could potentially give birth to a new universe. 

Now compare that to the Arizal’s teaching: 

Before creation, there was only Ein Sof — Infinite Divine Light. In order for finite reality to exist, Hashem performed Tzimtzum — concealing His infinite presence and creating a “space” (chalal panui) where creation could unfold. After the concealment, a thin ray of light — the kav — entered that space and began building structure through the Sefirot and the worlds. 

The structure is striking: 

• Contraction before expansion 
• Hidden interior before revelation 
• Darkness before light 
• Limited, measured emergence 
• Orientation and direction 

Black holes trap nearly all light — yet sometimes powerful jets burst outward. When black holes merge, they emit gravitational waves — ripples in spacetime that scientists detected for the first time in 2015. We did not see the collision. We heard it. 

Even in total darkness, something emerges. 

In Kabbalah, Tzimtzum does not mean absence — it means concealment. A reshimu, a trace, remains. The Infinite is hidden, not gone. 

Both frameworks suggest that what appears to be destruction may actually be preparation. What looks like emptiness may be the beginning of structure. What feels like darkness may be the womb of light. 

This lecture covers: 

– Black hole formation and rotation 
– The possibility of a spinning universe 
– Universe inside a black hole theory 
– Tzimtzum explained clearly 
– The kav and Divine structure 
– Concealment as creative force 
– Gravitational waves as echoes from hidden realms 
– Philosophical implications for faith and science 

Is this proof of anything? No. 

But it reveals something powerful: 

Both science and Kabbalah describe a reality where creation begins with contraction. 

Not explosion first — but concealment first. 

Before revelation, there is hiddenness. 
Before light, there is darkness. 
Before expansion, there is inward collapse. 

And that pattern may not only explain the cosmos. 

It may explain our lives.

snippet.title: Serah bat Asher — Guardian of Redemption and Memory – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Serah bat Asher is one of the most mysterious and powerful figures in all of Jewish history, yet the Torah mentions her only briefly. Beneath those short verses lies a breathtaking portrait of a woman who carried the spiritual memory of Klal Yisrael across centuries — from the house of Yaakov to the slavery in Egypt, from the Exodus to the splitting of the sea, and even into the era of King David. 

Why does the Torah name her among the seventy souls who descended to Egypt? Why is she the only granddaughter listed explicitly in that genealogy? And why does her name reappear generations later, as if time itself could not erase her presence? 

Chazal understood that Serah bat Asher was not merely part of the family — she was the living thread that held the generations together. When the Torah repeats her name in the census in Bamidbar, long after the descent into Egypt, the Midrash teaches that this is the very same Serah. She lived through the entire exile. She witnessed slavery. She stood at the Exodus. She crossed the sea. She entered the Land. 

But her greatness is not measured in years — it is measured in responsibility. 

When Yosef’s brothers returned from Egypt and needed to tell Yaakov that Yosef was still alive, they feared that the shock would overwhelm him. It was Serah who approached gently, who sang the message instead of declaring it. Through music and wisdom, she restored Yaakov’s spirit and brought back Ruach HaKodesh. In that moment, she became the guardian of hope. According to the Midrash, Yaakov blessed her that death would not rule over her — because she had revived his soul. 

Later, when Moshe appeared as the redeemer and proclaimed the words “Pakod Pakadti,” it was Serah who confirmed his authenticity. The elders did not rely on miracles alone. They turned to her — the keeper of the tradition passed down from Yosef. She recognized the secret phrase of redemption and declared that this was the true messenger of Hashem. Without her testimony, the redemption may not have been accepted. 

And when the time came to leave Egypt, it was Serah who revealed where Yosef’s coffin had been hidden in the Nile. Without fulfilling the oath to Yosef, the Exodus could not proceed. Once again, she completed what was missing. 

Throughout Midrash and Zohar, Serah bat Asher represents continuity. She corrects descriptions of Kriat Yam Suf, reminding the sages that unity remained even when the tribes walked in separate paths. She is identified as the wise woman who saved her city in the days of King David. She is counted among the few who entered Gan Eden alive. 

Kabbalah connects her to the letter Pe — the letter of “Pakod,” the sound of redemption. The Arizal teaches that even saying the verse that mentions her name carries spiritual protection. Across traditions, including Persian Jewish lore, she appears again and again as the woman who never truly left her people. 

Serah bat Asher teaches that redemption depends on memory. Without preserved words, without faithful transmission, without gentle wisdom in moments of crisis, history collapses. She embodies the idea that holiness does not fade when it is carried with responsibility. She shows that sometimes the most powerful figures are not the loudest leaders, but the quiet guardians of truth. 

Her story is not only about longevity — it is about spiritual endurance. It is about protecting the covenant across time. It is about ensuring that when the moment of redemption arrives, the people are ready to recognize it.

What if modern quantum physics is uncovering the very same truth that the Torah revealed thousands of years ago? What if the “Heavenly Ledger” described by our Sages is not just a moral metaphor—but the literal architecture of reality itself? 

In this groundbreaking lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the astonishing convergence between Torah wisdom and cutting-edge science. For generations, we have learned the powerful words from Pirkei Avot: “An eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds are written in a book.” We were taught that the ledger is open and the hand writes. These teachings shaped our understanding of Hashgacha Pratit, Divine Providence, and personal responsibility. But what if these statements are not poetic symbolism? What if they describe the fundamental structure of the universe? 

This class dives deep into one of the most perplexing problems in theoretical physics: the Black Hole Information Paradox. Modern physicists struggle with a central question in quantum mechanics—can information ever truly be destroyed? The emerging scientific consensus is extraordinary: information is never lost. Even when matter disappears into a black hole, the information encoded within it remains preserved on the event horizon. The universe itself appears to function like a perfect, indestructible recording system. 

Now consider the Torah perspective. From the Zohar to Lurianic Kabbalah, from the Maharal of Prague to the Baal Shem Tov, Jewish mystical tradition has long described reality as layered with spiritual imprint and permanent trace. The concept of Reshimu teaches that every spiritual action leaves an eternal mark. Every thought, every word, every deed creates a lasting imprint in the cosmic structure. The world is not a temporary stage—it is a dynamic recording field. 

In this lecture, we carefully examine how the quantum principle of information conservation mirrors the Torah’s teaching that nothing is ever erased. We explore how the “Book of Remembrance” described by our Sages aligns conceptually with the idea that the boundary of a black hole stores encoded information. We analyze how the Neshama, the eternal soul, functions within a universe that never deletes data. And we discuss how Techiyat HaMetim—the Resurrection of the Dead—can be understood through the lens of ultimate information recovery. 

This is not a superficial comparison between science and religion. It is a deep, disciplined exploration of how Torah and quantum physics may be describing the same underlying system from different languages. The Black Hole Information Paradox becomes more than a physics puzzle—it becomes a window into Divine Providence. Hashgacha is no longer abstract; it is woven into the quantum fabric of existence. 

For serious students of Torah, this class offers a powerful strengthening of emunah grounded in intellectual rigor. For seekers of science, it presents a framework in which faith and physics are not enemies but partners in truth. The Eternal Torah Record is not mythology—it may be the operating system of creation. 

If quantum mechanics teaches that no information can ever be destroyed, then every human action carries infinite weight. Every struggle, every hidden act of integrity, every quiet moment of growth is permanently encoded into reality. Nothing vanishes. Nothing is forgotten. The ledger is open.

snippet.description:

Is the universe slowly erasing you—or is it recording you with absolute precision? What if the deepest fear of humanity—that our lives fade into nothing—is directly contradicted by both quantum physics and the Eternal Torah? 

In this second installment of The Quantum Ledger series, Rav Eliyahu Bari takes us into the heart of a revolutionary convergence between modern science and ancient Jewish wisdom. Humanity has always struggled with the anxiety that time is a destroyer, that memory fades, and that identity dissolves into the past. If nothing leaves a permanent trace, morality becomes fragile. Justice becomes uncertain. Meaning becomes negotiable. 

The Torah responded to this fear thousands of years ago with a radical declaration: “All your deeds are written in a book.” This is not merely poetic imagery. It is a theological assertion that reality itself contains a perfect moral accounting. Every action, every intention, every exertion of will is permanently inscribed within the structure of existence. The “Sefer,” the Heavenly Book, represents a dimension of reality that cannot be corrupted or erased. 

Meanwhile, modern physics arrived at a strikingly similar conclusion—but through equations instead of prophecy. In quantum mechanics, one of the most fundamental principles is Unitarity. This law states that the evolution of a quantum system is fully reversible. Probabilities are conserved. The total information describing a system can never vanish. If one had perfect access to the universe’s data, one could theoretically rewind events to their precise origin. 

Physicists even formalized this idea through what is known as the No-Hiding Theorem. This theorem demonstrates that information cannot be destroyed and cannot be completely concealed. It can be scrambled, redistributed, encoded in different forms—but it can never be eliminated. The universe, at its most basic level, refuses to delete data. 

Here we encounter a profound alignment with Torah thought. When the Sages spoke about a “Pinkas,” a Ledger, they were not describing a physical notebook in the sky. They were revealing that reality itself contains a hidden dimension of exact accounting. Jewish mystical tradition describes existence as layered with spiritual imprint. Every choice produces consequence not only in the visible world, but in the informational fabric of creation. 

This is where the concept of Da’at Elyon—Supernal Knowledge—becomes transformative. God does not “remember” the way humans remember. Memory implies time, and the Creator stands beyond time. Instead, existence itself persists because it is known. Divine Providence, Hashgacha, is not surveillance. It is an active, continuous feedback loop between human free will and the eternal informational structure of reality. 

When quantum physics declares that information is never lost, and the Torah declares that every deed is eternally written, we are forced to reconsider the nature of accountability. Morality is not sustained by social agreement alone. It is built into the operating system of the cosmos. The universe is not morally neutral. It is informationally exact. 

This lecture carefully bridges scientific rigor with Torah depth. We break down Unitarity in accessible language. We explain how conservation of information reshapes our understanding of physical law. Then we map these principles onto the Torah’s description of the Eternal Ledger. The convergence is not superficial—it is structural. Two radically different intellectual traditions are pointing toward the same conclusion: nothing you do disappears. 

And this leads to the inevitable question: what happens when something appears to be destroyed? What about the most violent, extreme objects in existence—black holes? If anything in the universe could erase information, it would be them. Yet modern physics has discovered something astonishing. 

In the next part of this series, we will confront the Black Hole Information Paradox and see how a crisis in physics forced scientists to reaffirm the very principle the Torah has always taught: reality does not forget.

snippet.title: Quantum Physics in Pirkei Avot 3/8 – Ethics of Our Fathers – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Can even a black hole erase reality—or does the universe protect every fragment of information forever? What if the most destructive forces in existence actually prove the Torah’s teaching that the soul and its actions are indestructible? 

In this powerful continuation of The Quantum Ledger series, Rav Eliyahu Bari takes us into the heart of one of the greatest crises in modern physics: the Black Hole Information Paradox. We begin with a simple but unsettling image. Imagine burning an entire library to ash. Intuitively, we assume the knowledge is gone forever. Yet quantum mechanics insists otherwise. If one could gather every particle of smoke and every atom of residue, the original information could, in principle, be reconstructed. Information is never lost. 

Then came the challenge. In the 1970s, the study of black holes shook this foundational rule. According to Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity, a black hole possesses gravity so intense that nothing—not even light—can escape once it crosses the Event Horizon. For decades, scientists believed anything passing that boundary was permanently cut off from the universe. 

But Stephen Hawking introduced a revolutionary discovery: black holes emit radiation and slowly evaporate. Over unimaginable spans of time, they disappear. This triggered a scientific earthquake. If a black hole swallows information and then evaporates into random thermal radiation, it would seem that the information is destroyed. The universe’s “rewind button,” guaranteed by quantum mechanics, would be broken. The cosmic ledger would fail. 

This tension became known as the Black Hole Information Paradox. For a moment in scientific history, it appeared that the universe might truly forget. 

Yet physics did not surrender. Through decades of intense debate and mathematical development, researchers arrived at a breathtaking insight: the Holographic Principle. Rather than being lost inside the black hole’s singularity, the information of any object that falls inward becomes encoded on the two-dimensional surface of the black hole—the Event Horizon itself. The surface acts as a storage boundary. Every interaction leaves a precise informational imprint. 

In other words, the black hole does not destroy the data. It records it. 

Further developments, including calculations known as the Page Curve, demonstrated that as a black hole evaporates, the information is not erased. It slowly leaks back into the universe in an extraordinarily complex and encrypted form. The cosmos preserves its files. Even the most violent gravitational collapse cannot delete information; it can only transform and conceal it. 

Now pause and consider the Torah perspective. In Pirkei Avot, our Sages teach that “all your deeds are written in a book.” This is not a metaphor about ink and parchment. It is a description of system architecture. Reality itself contains a recording surface. The Heavenly Ledger is not a poetic exaggeration—it is the spiritual analogue of the informational boundary physicists discovered at the edge of black holes.

snippet.title: Quantum Physics in Pirkei Avot 5/8 – Ethics of Our Fathers – Rav Eliyahu Bari

If every action you take writes itself into the fabric of reality, where exactly is that information stored? What is the ultimate “hard drive” of the universe—and how did it come into existence?

To allow a world of choice and moral responsibility to exist, a radical process occurred: Tzimtzum, a withdrawal or concealment of infinite light. This act formed a conceptual vacuum known as the Chalal, an “empty space” in which finite reality could emerge. 

But the Chalal was not truly empty. 

The Arizal offers a striking analogy. Imagine a jar filled with thick oil. When you pour the oil out, the jar appears empty—but a subtle residue clings to its walls. That residue still carries the essence and character of what once filled it. In Kabbalah, this indestructible residue is called the Reshimu—the Trace, the Impression. 

The Reshimu is not poetic symbolism. It is described as the foundational informational imprint of creation. Kabbalistic texts explain that the Reshimu consists of Otiyot—Letters. And letters are not abstract decorations. They are discrete units of structured meaning. In computational language, they function like bits and qubits, fundamental informational building blocks. The Reshimu is the encoded DNA of existence. 

Modern physics has arrived at a remarkably parallel concept. The Holographic Principle suggests that the information describing a three-dimensional region of space can be fully encoded on a two-dimensional boundary. Reality, in other words, may function like a vast projection from an informational surface. 

Lurianic Kabbalah describes an almost identical architecture. The physical universe unfolds within the Chalal, yet its structural information is embedded in the surrounding layer of the Reshimu. The boundary holds the code. The world is not self-generating; it is data-driven. 

This convergence between Torah and theoretical physics is not superficial metaphor. It points toward a shared structural intuition: information is more fundamental than matter. Just as black hole event horizons encode physical data, the Reshimu encodes spiritual and existential data. The universe is not built from randomness—it is built from structured divine information. 

And here is where it becomes personal. 

Every time you act in the physical world, you generate energy, intention, and consequence. According to Torah thought, that energy interacts with the deeper informational layer of reality. Your deeds do not float away into nothingness. They interface with the Reshimu and modify its encoded pattern. The Cosmic Hard Drive is not static; it is responsive. 

When the Sages teach that “All your deeds are written in a book,” they are describing this very mechanism. The Book is not a celestial diary. It is the dynamic informational substrate of creation itself. Writing is not symbolic—it is ontological. Actions become code. 

From the perspective of quantum theory, interactions are never lost. Information is conserved. From the perspective of Kabbalah, spiritual impact is never erased. The Reshimu ensures continuity. Together, they describe a universe whose architecture preserves every meaningful imprint. 

This transforms our understanding of responsibility. We are not merely inhabitants of a prewritten system. We are participants in its ongoing compilation. Every choice contributes to the shaping of the cosmic record. The Trace left at the dawn of creation becomes the canvas upon which human freedom paints. 

In this lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari unpacks the depth of Or Ein Sof, Tzimtzum, Chalal, and Reshimu, connecting them with contemporary discussions about digital reality, holographic encoding, and information theory. The result is a breathtaking synthesis: Torah mysticism and modern physics both describe a universe grounded in indestructible informational structure. 

If the Reshimu is the ultimate hard drive of existence, then nothing truly disappears. The question that remains is even more astonishing: if our actions are encoded permanently, what about our identity? What about the Neshama itself? Is the human soul also a form of indestructible divine code?

We have already explored how physics insists that information is conserved, how black holes cannot destroy data, and how the Torah describes an Eternal Ledger that records every action. Now we turn inward. If the cosmos preserves information, what about the information that is you? 

Orthodox Jewish thought has long taught that the Neshama is eternal. But what does that actually mean? Rabbi Aryeh Kaplan—himself trained in physics before becoming one of the most lucid expositors of Kabbalah—offered a powerful analogy. The human body is hardware. It is a biological terminal, sophisticated yet temporary. The real “self”—your personality, your memories, your accumulated choices, your moral trajectory—is software. 

In modern computational language, software is not destroyed when a single device fails. If properly preserved, it can be restored, transferred, or instantiated elsewhere. Quantum information theory echoes this principle at a deeper level. Information patterns cannot simply vanish. They may transform, become encrypted, or change form—but deletion is not part of the system. 

From a Torah perspective, the ultimate “Master File” exists within Divine Knowledge. God does not remember the way humans remember. Rather, existence itself is sustained through His knowing. If every deed is written into the cosmic Book, then every identity is likewise preserved. Death is not annihilation of the self; it is the deactivation of local hardware while the core informational pattern remains intact. 

But what about thoughts? What about fleeting, silent ideas that never became speech or action? The Tanya, foundational to Chabad Hasidic philosophy, states unequivocally that no thought is ever lost. Thoughts generate spiritual letters. They create subtle imprints in the spiritual atmosphere. Nothing evaporates without trace. 

Physics presents a striking parallel in the No-Hiding Theorem. Internal states of a system cannot be completely concealed or destroyed. Even unobserved quantum states alter the total informational configuration of reality. The universe does not permit true erasure. The structure of reality is conservation-based. 

Contemporary thinkers have drawn an even deeper analogy between death and the crossing of an Event Horizon. To outside observers, a body decays. Entropy increases. Order dissolves into apparent chaos. But from the perspective of information theory, the underlying data is not destroyed. It is conserved within a different encoding framework. 

Imagine death not as deletion, but as relocation. The Neshama transitions from a localized biological system into a non-local informational state. Just as data can move from a physical hard drive into secure cloud storage, the soul shifts from embodied expression to higher-dimensional preservation. The entropy of the body does not imply the entropy of the self. 

This reframing radically alters how we view identity, accountability, and purpose. If your core self is indestructible information, then every choice you make becomes part of a permanent structure. Your growth is cumulative. Your struggles are meaningful. Your inner life matters eternally. 

In this lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari weaves together quantum conservation, Jewish mysticism, and philosophical clarity to show that the Torah’s doctrine of the eternal soul is not mystical escapism—it is consistent with the deepest laws of informational reality. The Neshama is not fragile biological output. It is structured divine code. 

And this leads to the ultimate question: if the informational pattern of the soul is perfectly preserved, can it ever be re-embodied? Can the divine “software” be reinstalled into renewed physical “hardware”? The Torah speaks of Techiyat HaMetim—the Resurrection of the Dead—as a future reality. Could this be understood as the ultimate act of information recovery? 

In the next part of this series, we will explore the mysterious concept of the Luz bone and uncover how Jewish tradition describes resurrection not as magic—but as restoration.

The Luz is not merely a mystical bone. It is the symbolic compression of identity. Techiyat HaMetim is not arbitrary revival. It is the ultimate download from the Divine Cloud. Teshuvah is not emotional relief. It is code-level editing within the Cosmic Ledger.

Why do the vast majority of observant Jews not wear tefillin on Chol HaMoed, despite strong sources suggesting they might? This video uncovers the deep halachic and Talmudic roots of one of the most fascinating and consequential debates in Jewish law, revealing how a sugya evolves into widespread communal practice.
In this first installment of a five-part series, we explore the foundational question: what is the true status of Chol HaMoed? The discussion begins with a universally accepted premise—tefillin are not worn on Shabbat and Yom Tov because they are themselves an אות (a sign), making the additional “sign” of tefillin unnecessary. However, Chol HaMoed occupies a unique and ambiguous position. Is it fundamentally a continuation of the festival with intrinsic sanctity, or does it retain enough weekday character to still require tefillin?
We analyze the key Talmudic principle from Menachot 36b, associated with Rabbi Akiva, which establishes that tefillin are worn only on days that require a sign, excluding days that inherently function as a sign. This principle appears straightforward, yet its application to Chol HaMoed is anything but simple. The sugya leaves room for interpretation, opening the door to divergent halachic conclusions.
The discussion becomes more nuanced through Moed Katan 18b, where Rabbi Yehudah permits writing tefillin on Chol HaMoed. This passage becomes a critical point of analysis among the Rishonim. Does the allowance imply relevance—that tefillin are meant to be worn during Chol HaMoed—or is it merely a practical concession for post-festival use? We explore both readings and demonstrate how even subtle textual implications can shape major halachic positions.
The Yerushalmi further intensifies the debate, as some Rishonim interpret it as stronger support for wearing tefillin on Chol HaMoed. The Rosh develops this perspective, arguing for continuity with weekday obligations. In contrast, other Rishonim emphasize the inherent sanctity of Chol HaMoed, pointing to mitzvot like sukkah on Sukkot and the prohibition of chametz on Pesach as evidence that the day itself carries covenantal significance. According to this view, Chol HaMoed is already an אות, and tefillin are therefore unnecessary.
This disagreement is ultimately codified in halachic practice. The Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim 31:2) rules that tefillin are not worn on Chol HaMoed, aligning with the view that the day itself is a sign. The Rema, however, records the Ashkenazic custom of wearing tefillin, while also acknowledging the complexity surrounding the recitation of a berachah. This divergence lays the groundwork for the striking reality of modern practice, where communities follow sharply different minhagim.
Beyond the technical halachic analysis, this video frames a broader and more compelling question: how does a theoretical dispute in the Talmud evolve into a near-universal practice among contemporary Orthodox Jews? As explored in Appendix A, nearly 90% of observant Jews today do not wear tefillin on Chol HaMoed. Understanding how this consensus developed requires tracing the full arc—from Talmudic principle, to Rishonim interpretation, to codified halachah, and finally to lived communal practice.

What if the question of tefillin on Chol HaMoed is not about obligation at all—but about spiritual reality? In this video, we move beyond the classic halachic debate and uncover how the Zohar and the Arizal fundamentally redefine the issue, transforming it from a legal uncertainty into a statement about spiritual status.
In Part 2 of this series, we introduce the mystical framework that reshapes the entire discussion. On the halachic level, the debate can still be framed as a safek: is Chol HaMoed considered enough of an אות (sign) to exempt tefillin, or does it remain close enough to weekday life to require them? But the Zohar and the Lurianic tradition shift the question entirely. They argue that the issue is not merely whether Chol HaMoed counts as a sign, but what kind of spiritual condition a person is already in during these ימים טובים.
We begin with the Zohar’s striking and deeply provocative claim. The Zohar does not simply classify Chol HaMoed as an אות—it declares that these days are themselves תפילין דמרי עלמא, the tefillin of the Master of the world. This is not metaphorical language alone; it carries concrete halachic and spiritual implications. The Zohar goes further, stating אסור לאעברא תפילין דמארי עלמא ולאנחא תפילין אחרנין—that it is forbidden to remove the tefillin of the Master of the world and replace them with human tefillin. It concludes with an intense expression that underscores the severity of the act. In the next video, we will carefully analyze this dramatic language, its meaning, and how it should be understood within the broader system of Torah thought.
We then turn to the Arizal, who articulates a parallel idea through a different conceptual lens. Rather than focusing on symbolic identity, the Arizal describes a shift in spiritual structure. He writes ולפיכך אין מניחין תפילין בחול המועד כלל—therefore, tefillin are not worn on Chol HaMoed at all—because שניהם עולים למעלה ממקום התפילין, both rise above the place of tefillin. In this formulation, Chol HaMoed is not lacking the mitzvah of tefillin. Instead, it transcends the level at which tefillin operate during the weekday. The implication is profound: wearing tefillin on Chol HaMoed would not add holiness—it would misalign with a higher spiritual state already present.
Despite their different language and emphasis, both the Zohar and the Arizal converge on a shared conclusion. The Zohar emphasizes the concept of the king’s seal, portraying Chol HaMoed as a divine imprint that should not be replaced by a lesser, human-made sign. The Arizal emphasizes elevation, explaining that the entire spiritual framework of these days exists above the ordinary plane of tefillin. Yet both insist on the same core idea: not wearing tefillin on Chol HaMoed is not a deficiency—it is a recognition of an already elevated reality.
This shift has enormous implications for how we understand both halacha and minhag. It helps explain why, over time, many communities moved toward not wearing tefillin on Chol HaMoed—not merely as a cautious halachic position, but as an expression of a deeper spiritual sensitivity rooted in Kabbalah. snippet.title: Tefillin on Chol HaMoed 3/5 – The King’s Seal in the Zohar – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltD4pW6DRpkIzGTv3V6PoNi

What does the Zohar really mean when it says that Chol HaMoed itself is “tefillin of the Master of the world”? And why does it use such intense language to describe wearing tefillin on these days? In this video, we slow down and carefully unpack one of the most powerful and misunderstood passages in the Zohar, revealing a profound spiritual model behind the halachic practice.
In Part 3 of this series, we focus on the full Zoharic text (Midrash HaNe’elam on Shir HaShirim, cited in Beit Yosef, Orach Chaim 31) and present both the original Hebrew and a precise English translation. This is essential, because the Zohar’s argument depends not only on its conclusion, but on the structure of its mashal—the parable of the king’s seal—which carries the core meaning of the entire passage.
The Zohar begins with a bold claim: Chol HaMoed is not merely like tefillin—it is תפילין דמרי עלמא, the tefillin of the Master of the world. These days are described as “supernal tefillin” resting upon the heads of Israel. From this premise, the Zohar draws a sharp conclusion: it is forbidden to remove these divine tefillin and replace them with human tefillin, which it describes as only a lower likeness or image. This contrast between higher and lower forms becomes the key to understanding the entire passage.
To explain this idea, the Zohar introduces the mashal of the king’s seal. At first, the king gives his servant an image of his seal—a representation that carries authority and inspires fear. This corresponds to weekday tefillin, which serve as a powerful sign of connection between האדם and the Divine. But then, out of greater love, the king gives the servant the actual royal seal itself—the original, higher reality. At that moment, the servant must set aside the image he created, because it has been replaced by something greater.
The Zohar’s dramatic warning emerges from this turning point. If the servant were to reject the king’s higher seal in favor of the image he himself made, it would not be an act of devotion—it would be a failure to recognize the king’s gift. The strong language—describing such a servant as deserving severe consequences—is not meant to diminish the holiness of tefillin. On the contrary, it elevates the status of Chol HaMoed. The message is clear: when a higher divine presence is already resting upon a person, insisting on a lower symbolic form becomes a distortion rather than an enhancement.
This reframes the entire question of tefillin on Chol HaMoed. According to the Zohar, the issue is not whether tefillin are permitted or even obligatory. The issue is whether wearing them reflects an accurate understanding of the spiritual reality of the day. Chol HaMoed is not an empty middle ground between weekday and Yom Tov. It is a זמן in which the Jew is already marked by a higher “seal,” a deeper level of divine closeness that renders the usual external sign unnecessary.
This perspective helps explain why the Zohar uses such vivid and forceful imagery. It is not engaging in polemic; it is teaching a principle: spiritual growth requires the ability to recognize when one level has been transcended by another. The mashal of the king’s seal captures that transition with precision and emotional force.

3. Why replacing a higher sign with a lower one is problematic

snippet.title: Tefillin on Chol HaMoed 5/5 – The Final Answer – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltD4pW6DRpkIzGTv3V6PoNi

Why does the debate about tefillin on Chol HaMoed begin in halacha—but end in a revelation about the nature of holiness itself? In this final video, we bring together the full picture, integrating the Talmudic, halachic, and mystical dimensions into one clear and powerful conclusion.
After exploring the sugya, the Rishonim, the Zohar, and the Arizal, we can now understand that this is not just a technical disagreement—it is a layered question about how holiness is expressed and experienced. On the halachic level, the issue is whether Chol HaMoed qualifies as an אות, a covenantal sign strong enough to exempt tefillin. This is why the Rishonim divide. Some see Chol HaMoed as inherently marked by mitzvot such as sukkah or the prohibition of chametz, giving it the status of an אות. Others read the Talmudic sources as leaving space for tefillin to continue, preserving a connection to weekday avodah.
But the discussion does not remain there. The Zohar enters and fundamentally transforms the question. It teaches that Chol HaMoed is not merely a candidate for the category of אות—it is itself a higher form of tefillin, a divine imprint resting upon the Jewish people. This is expressed through the powerful image of the king’s seal, where a higher reality replaces the need for a lower symbolic representation.
The Arizal then provides the inner structure behind this idea. He explains that on Chol HaMoed, the entire spiritual configuration rises above the usual מקום of tefillin. What tefillin accomplish during the weekday—drawing holiness into defined channels—is already surpassed by the elevation of the day itself. The absence of tefillin is therefore not a lack, and not even a compromise. It is a direct reflection of a higher state.
This synthesis gives new depth to the concept of אות. In the language of halacha, an אות is a sign—a marker of covenantal identity between a Jew and HaKadosh Baruch Hu. But in the language of sod, an אות is not just a symbol. It is a real spiritual imprint, an active condition in which a person stands. On Chol HaMoed, the mystical tradition teaches that a Jew is already בתוך האות—within the sign itself. The day does not merely remind him of holiness; it carries him בתוך a higher closeness.
From here emerges a profound lesson in avodat Hashem. Most of the time, a Jew serves by acting—by putting on tefillin, by taking hold of mitzvot, by actively drawing holiness into life. But there are moments when the עבודה shifts. There are times when the highest form of service is not to add, but to recognize. Not to grasp, but to stand בתוך what has already been given.
Chol HaMoed becomes the model for this kind of avodah. It teaches that spiritual growth is not only about doing more, but about perceiving more deeply. The discipline of restraint—of not adding an act when it is no longer aligned with the spiritual reality—is itself an expression of אמת and יראה.
This is why the practice developed as it did across much of the Jewish world. The convergence of halachic reasoning and mystical insight led many communities to experience Chol HaMoed not as an in-between זמן, but as a day of elevated presence—one in which the usual signs give way to a higher imprint.

3. The avodah of recognizing holiness instead of adding to it
