snippet.title: Tefillin on Chol HaMoed 4/5 – Lurianic Kabbalah – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltD4pW6DRpkIzGTv3V6PoNi

What does it actually mean to say that Chol HaMoed is “above” the level of tefillin? In this video, we move from the symbolic language of the Zohar to the precise spiritual system of the Arizal, uncovering a structured and deeply layered explanation of why tefillin are not worn on Chol HaMoed.
In Part 4 of this series, we study the full Lurianic passage from Sha’ar HaKavanot and Pri Etz Chaim, presenting both the original Hebrew and a clear English translation. The Arizal does not rely on metaphor alone—he describes a detailed spiritual configuration that explains how different ימים טובים affect the inner structure of the soul and the upper worlds.
The Arizal begins by comparing Chol HaMoed to Rosh Chodesh. On Rosh Chodesh, only a partial elevation occurs—the “head” rises to a higher level, which is why tefillin are still worn for most of the day and removed only during Musaf. This indicates that the spiritual influx temporarily exceeds the level of tefillin but does not fully replace it. Chol HaMoed, however, is fundamentally different. Here, the entire configuration shifts upward.
Using precise Kabbalistic terminology, the Arizal explains that during Chol HaMoed, both the “head” and the lower aspects of the spiritual structure ascend to a higher מקום. The imagery is striking: the heads are described as being “in the embrace of their Father,” while the rest of the structure rearranges accordingly. This is not poetic language—it reflects a reordering of spiritual levels in which the usual מקום of tefillin is no longer the operative plane.
This leads directly to the Arizal’s clear halachic conclusion: ולפיכך אין מניחין תפילין בחול המועד כלל—therefore, one does not put on tefillin on Chol HaMoed at all. The reason is not absence, but elevation. Tefillin correspond to a specific spiritual function tied to weekday reality, where distinct levels—such as מוחין and the relationship between “bridegroom” and “bride”—are expressed through defined channels. On Chol HaMoed, however, those distinctions are lifted into a higher unity, where the usual mechanisms of tefillin are no longer necessary.
The Arizal further explains that tefillin represent a structured relationship within the עולם of Atzilut, involving the transmission of divine intellect and flow through specific sefirotic arrangements. But on Chol HaMoed, both sides of that relationship rise above the מקום of that interaction. When the entire system is elevated, the כלי designed for a lower level is naturally set aside.
This idea transforms how we understand the absence of tefillin. It is not a suspension of a mitzvah due to uncertainty or compromise. It is a reflection of a different spiritual מצב altogether. The day itself carries the person into a higher framework, where the usual expressions of connection are replaced by a more direct and encompassing closeness.
This perspective also deepens the connection between halacha and Kabbalah. The Arizal is not introducing a new practice disconnected from earlier sources. He is revealing the פנימיות—the inner structure—behind a practice that already exists within the halachic tradition. His language gives conceptual clarity to what the Zohar expresses through metaphor, showing how elevation, rather than exemption, lies at the heart of Chol HaMoed.

2. Why tefillin belong to a lower defined spiritual level

snippet.title: Pesach Seder & Tefillin Shel Rosh 1/6 – The Crown of Redemption – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltlQ3tpgxCWWHWkuxWoDjO3

What is the deep connection between the Pesach Seder and the Tefillin Shel Rosh, and how does this relationship reveal the true meaning of the Crown of Redemption? In this powerful and eye-opening class, Rav Eliyahu Bari uncovers a profound spiritual link that transforms how we understand both Pesach and the daily mitzvah of Tefillin.

The Pesach Seder is not just a commemoration of the Exodus from Egypt—it is a living, experiential journey of redemption. Every element of the Seder is designed to awaken awareness, reshape identity, and guide a person through an internal process of liberation. But what happens after the Seder night ends? How is that redemption carried forward into daily life? This is where the connection to Tefillin Shel Rosh becomes essential.

Tefillin Shel Rosh, worn on the head, represents clarity of thought, alignment of the mind, and the elevation of consciousness. It is often described as a form of a “crown,” resting above a person’s intellect and symbolizing higher awareness. Rav Eliyahu Bari explains that just as the Pesach Seder initiates the process of redemption, the Tefillin Shel Rosh sustains and completes it on a daily basis.

The concept of the Crown of Redemption emerges from this connection. The Seder night plants the seeds of freedom, but the true “crown” is achieved when those insights are internalized and consistently expressed in everyday life. The Tefillin Shel Rosh serves as a daily reminder that redemption is not a one-time event, but an ongoing state of consciousness that must be maintained and renewed.

This class explores how the structure of the Pesach Seder mirrors the structure of spiritual growth. Each step—from telling the story to eating matzah—parallels stages of internal transformation. Rav Eliyahu Bari shows how these stages correspond to the role of Tefillin Shel Rosh, which binds a person’s thoughts to higher purpose and anchors redemption in the mind.

Another key insight revealed in this lesson is the idea that true freedom is intellectual and spiritual before it is physical. The Exodus was not only about leaving Egypt, but about removing the limitations of perception and belief. Tefillin Shel Rosh represents this transformation of the mind, turning abstract inspiration into structured awareness and disciplined thinking.

By understanding the connection between the Pesach Seder and Tefillin Shel Rosh, a person gains a practical framework for living redemption every day. The Crown of Redemption is not distant or abstract—it is built through consistency, awareness, and the ability to carry moments of inspiration into daily action.

This class will give you a deeper appreciation of both Pesach and Tefillin, revealing how these two mitzvot are intimately connected in guiding a person toward spiritual completion. It offers a powerful perspective on how to move from inspiration to integration, and from momentary insight to lasting transformation.

How Tefillin Shel Rosh represents the “crown” of spiritual awareness

The concept of the Crown of Redemption emerges from this connection. The Seder night plants the seeds of freedom, but the true “crown” is achieved when those insights are internalized and consistently expressed in everyday life. The Tefillin Shel Rosh serves as a daily reminder that redemption is not a one-time event, but an ongoing state of consciousness that must be maintained and renewed.

This class explores how the structure of the Pesach Seder mirrors the structure of spiritual growth. Each step—from telling the story to eating matzah—parallels stages of internal transformation. Rav Eliyahu Bari shows how these stages correspond to the role of Tefillin Shel Rosh, which binds a person’s thoughts to higher purpose and anchors redemption in the mind.

Another key insight revealed in this lesson is the idea that true freedom is intellectual and spiritual before it is physical. The Exodus was not only about leaving Egypt, but about removing the limitations of perception and belief. Tefillin Shel Rosh represents this transformation of the mind, turning abstract inspiration into structured awareness and disciplined thinking.

By understanding the connection between the Pesach Seder and Tefillin Shel Rosh, a person gains a practical framework for living redemption every day. The Crown of Redemption is not distant or abstract—it is built through consistency, awareness, and the ability to carry moments of inspiration into daily action.

This class will give you a deeper appreciation of both Pesach and Tefillin, revealing how these two mitzvot are intimately connected in guiding a person toward spiritual completion. It offers a powerful perspective on how to move from inspiration to integration, and from momentary insight to lasting transformation.

snippet.title: Ohr HaChaim – Emor – The Kohen’s Daughter and the Soul – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
In this English Torah class on Ohr HaChaim HaKadosh, Parshat Emor, Rav Eliyahu Bari  explains the deep remez hidden in the verses about who may eat from the holy foods. What appears at first to be a law about Kohanim, outsiders, servants, and a Kohen’s daughter becomes a powerful teaching about the soul, spiritual nourishment, sin, holiness, and the heavenly kodesh that sustains the Jewish people.
Ohr HaChaim begins by showing that the word “holy” has two layers. On the level of peshat, it refers to the sanctified foods of the sacrifices, which may not be eaten by a non-Kohen. But on the level of remez, kodesh refers to a higher spiritual sustenance from Heaven. This holy bounty is not merely food; it is the divine life-force that nourishes the soul according to its level, purity, and connection to Hashem.
The verse says that an “outsider” may not eat of the holy. Ohr HaChaim reads this as a spiritual principle: not every force, not every desire, and not every inner state can receive the nourishment called kodesh. Holy sustenance must be protected from the forces of impurity. If evil is attached to the soul, giving that soul access to kodesh would also strengthen the outsider clinging to it. Therefore, kodesh is reserved for those whose essence is goodness and whose inner life is aligned with holiness.
Rav Eliyahu Bari explains how Ohr HaChaim reads the Torah’s terms as allusions to the levels of the soul. The neshamah is compared to a Kohen because it is the highest of the three main levels: nefesh, ruach, and neshamah. The ruach is called the “seat” of the Kohen, because the neshamah rests upon the ruach. The nefesh is compared to a hired hand, because it activates human action, movement, effort, and practical life in this world.
At first, nefesh and ruach are not naturally fit to receive the lofty sustenance called kodesh. But when the neshamah elevates them through upright deeds, Torah study, mitzvot, and spiritual effort, even the nefesh can rise and become worthy of eating from the holy. This is one of the central ideas of the class: the lower parts of the soul can be lifted. A person is not trapped forever on the level where he begins. Through Torah and mitzvot, the neshamah can acquire the nefesh, refine it, and raise it to a higher spiritual state.
Ohr HaChaim then explains the phrase “someone born in his home.” This refers to holy sparks and souls that fell into the forces of impurity from ancient times, connected to Creation and Adam’s sin. The righteous, through their good deeds, can extract these sparks from the domain of evil. A mitzvah done by a righteous person acts like a magnet, drawing a spark of holiness out from its impure surroundings. These rescued sparks become like “offspring” of the neshamah that elevated them, and they too can rise to receive holy sustenance.
The class then turns to the Kohen’s daughter who marries an outsider. Ohr HaChaim explains this as a neshamah that has become blemished through its deeds and attached itself to the outsider, meaning the force of evil. When the soul follows the pleasures of impurity, it loses access to heavenly kodesh. Its spiritual nourishment is reduced, its radiance is dimmed, and its dignity is diminished. This is not only punishment; it is the natural result of spiritual distance from holiness.
The final verse speaks about the Kohen’s daughter who becomes a widow or divorcee and returns to her father’s house. Ohr HaChaim reads this as an allusion to the neshamah’s neshamah, the highest soul-level discussed here. Evil cannot truly cling to it. Instead, when sin approaches, it detaches and leaves. This is hinted to by the cantillation mark called tilsha, meaning detached. The higher soul returns to its holy Source, unharmed by the sin itself, but without the earned spiritual independence it could have gained through mitzvot and good deeds.
This teaches a powerful lesson about free will and spiritual responsibility. A person can host a lofty soul, but if he violates Hashem’s word, he drives that holiness away. If he fails to produce spiritual fruit in this world, the soul returns to Heaven and must eat from the Father’s table as before, without the dignity of earned reward. By contrast, a soul elevated through Torah and mitzvot enjoys the fruit of its own labor.

snippet.title: Tree of Knowledge 1/8 – Was the Tree of Knowledge Wheat? – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3Ilv2pw0JZLha--hdGnDhZrWC

What if the first sin in Gan Eden was not only about disobedience, but about reaching for knowledge before the soul was ready to contain it? In this opening class of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, we explore one of Chazal’s most surprising opinions: the Tree of Knowledge was wheat.

Most people imagine the Tree as an apple or a mysterious forbidden fruit, but Chazal point us deeper. In Bereishit Rabbah 15:7, our Sages discuss several opinions about the identity of the Tree, and one view says it was wheat. At first, this seems strange. Wheat is not a tree. But Chazal are not giving us a botanical report. They are revealing a spiritual map of human development, maturity, awareness, and the danger of receiving da’at before its proper time.

The Gemara in Berachot 40a teaches that a child does not know how to call out “father” and “mother” until he tastes grain. Wheat is therefore connected to da’at — developed awareness, structured consciousness, and the ability to name reality. Wheat is not merely food. It represents the awakening of human intelligence and the beginning of ordered perception.

This changes the story of Adam and Chava. The sin was not simply eating something forbidden. It was reaching for a level of awareness before they were ready to live with it. Adam and Chava were meant to grow into knowledge. They were meant to receive da’at in the right way, at the right stage, with the proper inner vessels. Instead, they jumped ahead.

This is a powerful lesson for every serious student of Torah, personal growth, and Jewish thought. Knowledge is not always safe simply because it is true. More information does not always produce more wisdom. A person can encounter a real idea or powerful spiritual concept, but without the maturity to hold it properly, that knowledge may not elevate him. It may confuse him, destabilize him, make him cynical, or inflate his ego. Sometimes the problem is not falsehood. Sometimes the problem is truth without preparation.

That is the tragedy of wheat. Wheat is not evil. Grain is life-giving. Bread sustains the world. But even something good can become destructive when it is taken out of order. The issue is timing, readiness, vessel, and process. Adam and Chava reached for something powerful, but holiness without preparation can become dangerous because the soul must be built before it can carry higher awareness.

This class also opens a deeper way to understand the Tree of Knowledge in Torah and Chazal. The question is not only, “What fruit was it?” The deeper question is, “What kind of knowledge entered the human being?” In Sanhedrin 70a and related teachings of Chazal, the discussion of the Tree is connected to human awareness, desire, exposure, and the consequences of knowledge entering before the person is properly aligned.

Every generation faces this challenge. We live in a world where information is instant and access is unlimited. People are exposed to ideas long before they have the emotional, intellectual, and spiritual structure to process them. A person can know too much too soon. A person can hear sophisticated ideas before basic foundations are strong. A person can confuse exposure with wisdom, intensity with depth, and curiosity with readiness. Gan Eden speaks directly to this modern struggle.

Rav Eliyahu Bari explains that according to this view, the first sin was misaligned growth. It was not simple rebellion or hatred of Hashem. It was the desire to become more, faster than the soul was ready to become. Adam and Chava wanted da’at, but they took it before the proper time. They wanted expanded consciousness, but without the process needed to hold it. They wanted depth, but without the vessels.

The Tree of Knowledge teaches us that spiritual growth has an order. Wisdom must be received with humility. Awareness must be matched by character. Knowledge must be guided by Torah, maturity, and yirat Shamayim. The right truth at the wrong time can become harmful, while the same truth received properly can become a source of life.

snippet.title: Tree of Knowledge 2/8 – Did Wine Cause the First Sin? – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
What if the Tree of Knowledge was not only about forbidden knowledge, but about overwhelming experience? In Part 2 of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, we explore the astonishing opinion of Chazal that the Tree was a vine — and that wine played a central role in the first human sin.

In the previous class, Rav Eliyahu Bari explained the opinion that the Tree of Knowledge was wheat. Wheat represents process, structure, development, and da’at that must be prepared step by step. But now Chazal give us a very different image. In Sanhedrin 70a, one opinion teaches that the Tree from which Adam HaRishon ate was a vine. According to this view, the Tree of Knowledge was connected to wine.

This changes the entire atmosphere of Gan Eden. Wheat represents structured awareness. Wine represents emotional experience. Wheat develops slowly; wine enters directly. It bypasses the ordinary intellectual process and reaches the emotional center of the person. Wine loosens barriers, reveals hidden layers, and uncovers what was concealed beneath the surface.

This is why Chazal say in Eruvin 65a: “When wine enters, secrets come out.” Wine does not create something new from nothing. It exposes what is already inside. It can reveal joy, love, pain, desire, confusion, vulnerability, and truth. That is why wine is so powerful in Torah. It can be used for Kiddush, simcha, and sanctification, but it can also lead to exposure, downfall, and loss of boundaries.

According to this opinion, the sin of Adam and Chava was not only that they knew too soon. It was that they felt too much. The Tree of Knowledge was not merely premature intellect; it was uncontained experience. Adam and Chava were exposed to an intensity they were not yet prepared to hold. The experience entered the heart, imagination, body, and desire before the human vessel had the discipline and structure needed to contain it.

This is a different kind of danger. Knowledge can destabilize the mind, but experience can overwhelm the whole person. A person may hear an idea and remain composed. But when something is deeply felt, emotional, sensory, exciting, and intoxicating, it can change a person instantly. Wine teaches that not every powerful experience is automatically holy. Intensity can open the soul, but it can also flood it.

The Torah shows this pattern again after the Flood. Noach leaves the teivah, plants a vineyard, drinks wine, and becomes exposed. In Bereishit 9:20–24, wine is connected to revelation without boundaries. Noach survives the destruction of the world, begins again, and immediately the vineyard appears as a test of human vulnerability. Wine reveals, but if the person is not ready, revelation becomes exposure.

That is one of the deepest lessons of the Tree of Knowledge. The problem is not wine itself. Wine is not evil. Wine is used in mitzvot, celebration, Shabbat, Yom Tov, weddings, and moments of holiness. The problem is wine without vessels. The problem is intensity without preparation. A person can crave inspiration, spiritual emotion, mystical feeling, and powerful moments of connection, but without Torah, humility, restraint, and maturity, those experiences may not elevate him. They may simply intoxicate him.

This class is especially relevant in a generation that often confuses intensity with truth. If something feels powerful, many people assume it must be authentic. If something moves them emotionally, they assume it must be holy. But Chazal teach us a more careful approach. A strong feeling is not the same as spiritual truth. Emotional force is not the same as inner repair. Fire can warm, but fire can also burn.

Rav Eliyahu Bari explains that according to this opinion, the Tree of Knowledge was the vine because the first sin was the attempt to experience more than the human being was ready to contain. Adam and Chava reached for expansion, sensation, revelation, and emotional intensity before their inner world was properly aligned. The result was not elevation, but fracture; not clarity, but exposure; not sanctified depth, but overflow.

snippet.title: Tree of Knowledge 3/8 – Was the Tree of Knowledge a Fig? – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3Ilv2pw0JZLha--hdGnDhZrWC

What if the Tree of Knowledge did not only change what Adam and Chava knew, but changed the way they saw themselves? In Part 3 of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, we explore the opinion of Chazal that the Tree was the fig — the fruit connected to self-awareness, shame, identity, and the birth of the divided human psyche.

This opinion feels especially striking because the Torah itself seems to point in this direction. After Adam and Chava eat from the Tree, their eyes are opened, they realize they are naked, and they sew together fig leaves: “וַיִּתְפְּרוּ עֲלֵה תְאֵנָה.” Chazal understand that this was not random. According to the opinion in Berachot 40a, the Tree of Knowledge was the fig, and Bereishit Rabbah 15:7 teaches that with the very thing through which they damaged, they began to repair.

In the first video, we saw wheat: da’at, structured knowledge, and awareness before its proper time. In the second video, we saw wine: intensity, emotional experience, and revelation without vessels. Now the fig opens a third dimension. Wheat is intellect. Wine is experience. Fig is identity.

Before the sin, Bereishit 2:25 says Adam and Chava were naked and not ashamed. This does not simply mean they lacked clothing. It means they existed in wholeness. There was no painful split between inside and outside, no embarrassment, no insecurity, no self-consciousness, and no fear of being seen. Their outer appearance did not contradict their inner truth.

After the sin, everything changes. Bereishit 3:7 says their eyes were opened and they knew they were naked. This is not only the discovery of physical nakedness. It is the birth of self-consciousness. The human being begins to see himself from the outside. Once a person sees himself from the outside, he can judge himself, compare himself, evaluate himself, and feel exposed.

That gap becomes shame. Shame is not merely embarrassment. Shame is the feeling that the self has become fractured. A person is no longer simply living from within. He is now watching himself being seen. He becomes both the one who experiences life and the one who evaluates that experience. He develops an inner observer, an inner critic, and an inner fear.

According to this view, the fig represents the moment human identity becomes complicated. The Tree of Knowledge did not simply give Adam and Chava new information. It created a new relationship to the self. Before the sin, they were whole. After the sin, they became self-aware in a fractured way. They saw themselves, but that seeing produced distance, vulnerability, exposure, and a painful gap from perfection.

This is why the fig leaves matter. They are not merely the first clothing. They are the first human attempt to manage shame. Adam and Chava do not only cover their bodies; they try to cover their exposure. They try to control how they are seen. The fig leaves become the first symbol of concealment, image, self-protection, and the human effort to survive the pain of judgment.

And yet, Chazal reveal something very deep: the same thing through which they fell became the beginning of their repair. The fig is both the wound and the covering. The area where the damage appears becomes the place where tikkun begins. Shame, when understood properly, can become a doorway to growth. The awareness that I am not yet who I should be can destroy a person if it becomes despair, but it can also awaken responsibility, humility, teshuvah, and the desire to rebuild.

This class speaks directly to every person. We all know what it means to appear one way and feel another way. We all know what it means to be seen and feel exposed. We all know what it means to hide parts of ourselves because we fear judgment. We all know the gap between inner truth and outer presentation.

Rav Eliyahu Bari explains that according to this opinion, the Tree of Knowledge was the fig because the sin changed human identity itself. It introduced self-consciousness, shame, and the experience of being divided within oneself.

snippet.title: Tree of Knowledge 4/8 – Was the Tree of Knowledge an Etrog? – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
What if the Tree of Knowledge was not ugly, dark, or obviously sinful, but beautiful, refined, and spiritually compelling?

In Part 4 of Rav Eliyahu Bari's 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, we explore the opinion that the Tree was the etrog — and discover one of the deepest tests in avodas Hashem: confusing what appears good with what is truly right.

The first three parts of this series opened three dimensions of the first sin. Wheat represents premature knowledge — da'at before the soul is ready to contain it. Wine represents overwhelming experience — spiritual intensity without proper vessels. The fig represents self-awareness, shame, and the fractured way a person begins to see himself after the sin.

But the fourth opinion, identifying the Tree of Knowledge with the etrog, enters an even subtler area: perception itself.

The etrog is beautiful, fragrant, complete, and refined. It is connected to mitzvah, held on Sukkot as part of the arba minim, and associated with "pri etz hadar" in Vayikra 23:40. Some traditions, including Targum Yonatan to Bereishit 3:6, identify the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge with the etrog, placing this beautiful fruit at the center of the first human failure.

That is what makes this opinion so powerful. The sin did not necessarily begin with something that looked evil. It may have begun with something that looked completely good. Chava saw that the tree was good for eating, desirable to the eyes, and pleasant for gaining wisdom. The problem was not that it seemed destructive — it was that appearance became the measure of truth.

This is the danger of the etrog: misplaced good.

A person can choose something good in essence, but wrong in timing, context, intention, or alignment with the will of Hashem. Because the thing itself looks elevated, the mistake becomes harder to detect. It is easy to reject darkness when it appears as darkness. It is far more difficult to reject something that looks holy, sounds profound, feels inspiring — but is not what Hashem wants from you now.

The etrog teaches that even good needs boundaries. Even beauty needs command. Even spiritual desire needs submission to ratzon Hashem.

In avodas Hashem, this lesson is extremely relevant. A person can pursue something because it looks spiritual or feels holy — but feeling holy is not the same as being aligned with Hashem's will. The Tree of Knowledge, according to this opinion, exposes the danger of allowing beauty, emotion, and appearance to define what is right.

Rav Eliyahu Bari explains that this is not only a story about Adam and Chava. It is the story of every person who must learn to distinguish between spiritual appearance and spiritual truth. Sometimes the yetzer hara does not tempt a person with obvious rebellion. Sometimes it dresses the wrong choice in the clothing of beauty, growth, wisdom, and even holiness.

Bereishit 3:6 is central because the Torah describes the tree through perception: good for eating, desirable to the eyes, and pleasant for wisdom. But Torah teaches that truth is not defined by appearance. Holiness is measured by relationship to Hashem, obedience, humility, and proper order.

The etrog therefore reveals a fourth fracture caused by the Tree of Knowledge. Wheat is the fracture of knowledge before its time. Wine is the fracture of experience without vessels. Fig is the fracture of self-consciousness and shame. Etrog is the fracture of perception — confusing what looks good with what is truly right.

And yet, the etrog also points toward repair. On Sukkot, the etrog is not taken alone. It is held together with the lulav, hadasim, and aravot, as part of a mitzvah. Its beauty becomes holy when placed inside command, structure, and Divine service. Beauty outside the will of Hashem can mislead; beauty inside the will of Hashem can elevate.

snippet.title: Tree of Knowledge 5/8 – Four Fruits, One Tree of Knowledge – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
What if the four opinions of Chazal about the Tree of Knowledge are not competing answers, but four layers of one truth?

In Part 5 of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, we step back from wheat, wine, fig, and etrog to see how these four fruits form a complete spiritual map of the human being.

Until now, each class focused on one opinion. Wheat revealed the intellectual layer of the sin. Wine revealed the experiential and emotional layer. Fig revealed the psychological layer of shame and self-awareness. Etrog revealed the perceptual layer, where a person confuses what appears good with what is truly right.

Which one is correct? Was the Tree wheat, wine, fig, or etrog?

The answer is that all of them are true. They are mapping the human condition. Each opinion reveals another dimension of what happened when Adam and Chava ate from the Tree of Knowledge. The sin was a spiritual rupture that affected the mind, heart, self, and perception.

Wheat represents da’at, structured awareness, and the danger of knowledge before its proper time. As Chazal teach in Berachot 40a, a child does not know how to call out to father and mother until he tastes grain. Wheat symbolizes organized consciousness: the ability to name reality and understand relationships. But when knowledge comes before the vessel is ready, it destabilizes.

Wine represents experience, emotional intensity, and revelation without containment. In Sanhedrin 70a, Chazal identify the Tree with the vine. Wine loosens boundaries, reveals hidden things, and brings the inner world to the surface. It can be used for Kiddush and simcha, but it can also lead to exposure and downfall. Wine teaches that intensity is not the same as truth.

Fig represents self-awareness, shame, and fragmented identity. After the sin, Bereishit 3:7 says that Adam and Chava’s eyes were opened, they knew they were naked, and they sewed fig leaves together. According to the opinion that the Tree was the fig, the same thing through which they fell became the first covering of the fall. The fig reveals the divided self: the person who sees himself, judges himself, compares himself, and feels exposed.

Etrog represents perception, beauty, and the danger of misplaced good. Some sources, including Targum Yonatan to Bereishit 3:6, identify the Tree with the etrog. The etrog is beautiful, fragrant, refined, and connected to mitzvah through “pri etz hadar” in Vayikra 23:40. This teaches that the first sin may have appeared beautiful, wise, and elevated. The danger was mistaking what looked good for what was aligned with ratzon Hashem.

Together, these four opinions reveal that the Tree of Knowledge was not only about one act of eating. It was a cascade. The mind was affected through premature knowledge. The heart was affected through emotional overflow. The self was affected through shame and fragmentation. Perception was affected through the confusion between appearance and truth.

Every person lives within these four layers. We struggle with what we know, what we feel, how we see ourselves, and how we decide what is truly good. A person may know something but not be ready to hold it. A person may feel something intensely, but that feeling may not be truth. A person may become self-aware, but that awareness may turn into shame. A person may see something beautiful and assume it is right, even when it is not aligned with Hashem’s will.

This helps explain why the Torah calls it the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil — עץ הדעת טוב ורע. The problem is mixed knowledge, confused knowledge, and knowledge that no longer arrives with perfect clarity. After the sin, the human being must sort reality: Is this wisdom or arrogance? Is this feeling or truth? Is this shame or humility? Is this goodness, or only the appearance of goodness?

If we only had wheat, we might think the sin was intellectual. If we only had wine, we might think it was emotional. If we only had fig, we might think it was psychological. If we only had etrog, we might think it was perceptual. But Chazal give us all four because the Tree affected the whole human being.

Rav Eliyahu Bari explains that sometimes one subject is described through several opinions because each view reveals another layer of the same truth. Wheat, wine, fig, and etrog are four entrances into da’at tov v’ra, the mixed awareness that defines human life after Gan Eden.

snippet.title: Tree of Knowledge 6/8 – The Zohar on the Tree of Knowledge – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
What if the four opinions about the Tree of Knowledge are not four separate explanations, but four parts of one spiritual system?

In Part 6 of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, we enter the language of the Zohar and see how wheat, wine, fig, and etrog reveal one unified structure of human confusion, perception, and repair.

Until now, this series explored four symbolic layers. Wheat represents da’at, structured awareness, and knowledge before its proper time. Wine represents emotional intensity, revelation, overflow, and feeling more than the vessel can contain. Fig represents self-awareness, shame, exposure, and fragmented identity. Etrog represents perception: the confusion between what appears good and what is truly aligned with ratzon Hashem.

The Zohar lifts this discussion into a deeper dimension. Reality is not flat. It is layered, structured, and alive with inner relationships. Creation is built through worlds, sefirot, spiritual forces, and connections between higher and lower levels. What appears separate from below may be unified above. What looks like disagreement on the surface may be several expressions of one hidden root.

This changes how we learn the sugya of the Tree of Knowledge. A surface approach asks: which opinion is correct? Was the Tree wheat, wine, fig, or etrog? The Zohar teaches us to ask: what does each opinion reveal, and how do they fit together? The goal is not to flatten Chazal into one physical answer, but to understand the structure behind the disagreement. The Tree was where multiple dimensions converged.

Wheat, wine, fig, and etrog are layers of the human being. Wheat touches the mind. Wine touches the heart and emotional expansion. Fig touches identity and self-consciousness. Etrog touches perception, beauty, and the way a person evaluates what is good. The sin of Adam and Chava did not remain in one area. It moved through the whole human structure.

This is why the Torah calls it עץ הדעת טוב ורע — the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. The core issue is mixture. Good and evil are no longer perceived with perfect clarity. Reality becomes interwoven. Before the sin, the human being related to truth in a more direct way. After the sin, reality must be clarified. A person must ask: is this wisdom or arrogance? Is this inspiration or intoxication? Is this shame or humility? Is this beauty, or only the appearance of goodness?

The Zohar teaches us to stop thinking in fragments. Human confusion is not only intellectual, emotional, psychological, or perceptual. It is systemic. An idea enters the mind. A feeling attaches to it. The self begins to identify with it. Then perception becomes shaped around it. What began as one thought may become an emotional state, then an identity, then a worldview.

That is why the Tree of Knowledge is so central to Torah thought. It is not merely the story of the first mistake. It is the root pattern of mixed reality after Gan Eden. Every person lives inside this system. We know things, feel things, see ourselves through those feelings, and evaluate reality through that identity. When aligned, knowledge becomes wisdom, experience becomes avodas Hashem, self-awareness becomes humility, and perception becomes truth. When distorted, knowledge becomes arrogance, experience becomes overflow, self-awareness becomes shame, and perception becomes confusion.

Rav Eliyahu Bari explains that this is why all four opinions are necessary. If we only had wheat, we would think the Tree was about intellect alone. If only wine, emotion alone. If only fig, shame alone. If only etrog, appearance alone. The Zohar reveals that all four belong to one architecture.

This also gives us a new way to understand Torah learning. Torah is not learned by choosing the simplest surface explanation and discarding the rest. Often, Torah reveals itself through layers. Pshat, Midrash, Gemara, and Zohar do not always compete. They may disclose different dimensions of one reality. The question becomes: “What layer of truth is revealed?”

In the Zohar’s framework, the Tree of Knowledge becomes a key to human confusion. We seek wisdom, but can become arrogant. We seek inspiration, but can become intoxicated. We seek self-knowledge, but can become ashamed. We seek beauty and goodness, but can mistake appearance for truth. The work of life is to clarify the mixture and return each layer to alignment with Hashem.

--- IN THIS VIDEO ---

1. Why the four opinions form one system
2. How the Zohar explains the Tree
3. Practical takeaway for daily life

This is Part 6 of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, focusing on the Zohar’s way of seeing all four opinions as one spiritual system. Through Zohar I on Bereishit, Zohar I 27b–28a, Zohar I 36b, and Bereishit 2:9 and 3:6–7, this class explores how the first sin affected mind, heart, identity, and perception.

snippet.title: Tree of Knowledge 7/8 – The Tree of Knowledge Inside the Soul – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
What if the deepest result of the Tree of Knowledge was not only that the world changed, but that the human soul itself changed?

In Part 7 of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, we enter the teaching of the Arizal and explore what happened inside Adam HaRishon — and inside every human being after him.

In the previous class, we saw the Zohar’s approach: the four opinions of Chazal are parts of one spiritual system. Wheat, wine, fig, and etrog represent mind, emotion, identity, and perception. The Tree of Knowledge stands where these layers meet, and the first sin affected the entire human structure.

The Arizal now takes us deeper. The Zohar shows the system, but the Arizal asks what that system did to the soul. According to the Arizal in Etz Chaim and related teachings, before the sin, good and evil were not experienced as they are now. They were separate. The human being lived with greater clarity. Truth did not have to be excavated from confusion. Reality was more transparent, and the soul was more aligned.

After the sin, everything changed. Good and evil became mixed inside the human being. The struggle moved inward. It was no longer simply a choice between external good and external evil. The chooser himself became mixed. Man now contains clarity and confusion, sincerity and distortion, longing for holiness and attraction to what damages him.

This explains why human life feels so difficult. A person can want good and still feel pulled elsewhere, have sincere intentions and still misunderstand himself, feel something deeply and still be wrong. Very often, we are drawn to a mixture. We sense something real inside it, but do not know how to separate the good from the brokenness around it.

This is the Arizal’s language of birur — clarification, sorting, and separating. If good and evil are mixed, then the work of life is to separate them. This sorting happens inside the mind, heart, desire, identity, and perception. Life after Gan Eden becomes a process of birur: identifying the good, extracting it from confusion, rejecting distortion, and returning the spark to holiness.

Now we can reread the four fruits more deeply. Wheat means the mind became mixed: thought can contain wisdom and arrogance, insight and confusion, Torah and ego. Wine means emotion became mixed: inspiration may contain desire, escape, or self-intoxication. Fig means identity became mixed: self-awareness can lead to humility and teshuvah, but also shame and hiding. Etrog means perception became mixed: something may look beautiful, spiritual, and elevated, but still be misaligned with ratzon Hashem.

This is why moral struggle feels so personal. The battlefield is within us: in our reasoning, emotions, self-image, desires, and perception of what is good. We often stand inside a fog, trying to understand which part of a thought is truth and which part is ego, which part of a feeling is holiness and which part is impulse, which part of shame is humility and which part is despair.

Rav Eliyahu Bari explains that the Arizal’s teaching is not meant to create despair. It gives us a map. If the problem is mixture, the solution is birur. If the soul became confused, the work of life is to restore clarity. Through mitzvot, Torah, tefillah, self-honesty, and avodas Hashem, a person separates clarity from confusion and elevates sparks trapped inside the mixture.

This is why mitzvot are so central in the writings of the Arizal, including Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaMitzvot, and related teachings. Mitzvot are acts of birur. They elevate sparks and reconnect fragments of reality to their Divine root. When a person eats with kedushah, speaks with restraint, learns Torah with humility, gives tzedakah, keeps Shabbat, or performs a mitzvah with intention, he is helping repair the mixture created after Adam’s sin.

The Tree of Knowledge becomes the root of all inner work. Before the sin, good and evil were separate. After the sin, they became mixed within the human being. Every act of growth now requires discernment. Every step toward Hashem requires clarification. Every sincere person must ask: what is the good here, and what is the distortion? What is holy desire, and what is ego? What is truth, and what is merely attractive? What is a spark to elevate, and what is a shell to leave behind?

--- IN THIS VIDEO ---

1. What changed inside the human soul
2. The Arizal’s teaching on birur
3. How Torah and mitzvot repair the mixture

This is Part 7 of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, focusing on the Arizal’s teaching about what changed inside the soul after Adam’s sin. Through Etz Chaim, Shaar HaGilgulim, Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaMitzvot, and Bereishit 3, this class explores good and evil, birur, the inner battlefield, and the repair of the soul.

#TreeOfKnowledge #RavEliyahuBari #Arizal #TorahClass #JewishWisdom #GanEden #AdamHaRishon #Birur #TorahLearning #JewishThought

snippet.title: Tree of Knowledge 8/8 – How Do We Fix the Tree of Knowledge? – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
If the Tree of Knowledge created mixture, confusion, and inner fragmentation, how do we repair it?

In the final class of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s 8-part series on the Tree of Knowledge, we arrive at the central question: if good and evil became intertwined inside reality and inside the human being, what is the path back to truth?

The answer is one of the deepest foundations of Torah life: if the damage is mixture, the repair is clarification. If the sin created עירוב — a mixing of good and evil, truth and distortion, holiness and confusion — then the path of tikkun is בירור, the work of sorting, refining, elevating, and realigning. The human mission is to enter a mixed world, identify the sparks of good hidden within it, separate them from distortion, and reconnect them to Hashem.

This is the role of mitzvot. Mitzvot are not just rituals or routines. They are tools of alignment. They take a world confused after the sin of Adam HaRishon and begin to restore order. A mitzvah creates clarity inside mixed reality. It places an action, object, desire, word, thought, or resource back into its proper relationship with the will of Hashem.

When a person eats with a berachah, he is not only eating. He is taking physical energy and placing it into the service of Hashem. Food can remain appetite, or it can become strength for Torah, chesed, tefillah, family, patience, and avodas Hashem. The berachah clarifies the act and reminds us that the physical world is not separate from holiness.

When a person gives tzedakah, he is not only transferring money. He is taking material resources and turning them into chesed. Money can become ego, control, anxiety, or self-protection. Through tzedakah, that same money becomes kindness, compassion, responsibility, and partnership with Hashem’s world.

When a person learns Torah, he is not only gaining information. He is aligning the mind with Divine truth. After the Tree of Knowledge, the mind can become mixed. Knowledge can become arrogance. Intelligence can become self-importance. Ideas can become weapons. Torah learning repairs the mind by training it to receive truth with humility.

This is the process of tikkun: step by step, choice by choice, action by action. We take a world where good and evil are mixed and reveal the good hidden inside it. The repair of the Tree of Knowledge happens in daily life: speech, thought, business, food, family, learning, restraint, generosity, modesty, honesty, humility, and responsibility. Every mitzvah is a small act of reordering the world.

Rav Eliyahu Bari explains that this is why the teachings of Ramchal, Nefesh HaChaim, the Arizal, and Tanya are essential here. Ramchal in Derech Hashem explains that man has a role in perfecting himself and creation. Nefesh HaChaim teaches that human action below affects higher worlds. The Arizal describes mitzvot as acts of birur and elevation. Tanya explains that mitzvot refine the world and help make a dwelling for Hashem below.

These teachings reveal that Jewish action is never merely external. A mitzvah performed in this world carries cosmic meaning. A word of Torah, a berachah, an act of tzedakah, a moment of restraint, a choice to speak truth, forgive, honor Shabbat, or guard one’s eyes or tongue — these are not small private gestures. They are part of the repair of the mixture that entered reality after Gan Eden.

Now the entire series comes together. Wheat taught us that knowledge needs vessels. Wine taught us that experience needs boundaries. Fig taught us that self-awareness needs healing. Etrog taught us that goodness needs alignment. The Zohar taught us that all these layers are one system. The Arizal taught us that the mixture of good and evil is now inside us. And mitzvot teach us how to repair it.

The story of the Tree of Knowledge is not only about what went wrong long ago. It is about what every human being is here to fix now. We live after the Tree, inside a world of mixed motives, desires, perceptions, emotions, and knowledge. Our task is to bring clarity back into the places where confusion entered.

Torah life is practical because the repair is practical. It is in how we eat, speak, use money, think, treat others, learn, pray, respond when no one sees us, and align ordinary life with Hashem. Every mitzvah clarifies another point of reality. Every act of avodas Hashem separates another spark from confusion.

--- IN THIS VIDEO ---

1. How mitzvot repair the Tree of Knowledge
2. The meaning of tikkun and birur
3. Practical takeaway for daily life

This is Part 8, the final class in Rav Eliyahu Bari’s series. Through Ramchal’s Derech Hashem, Nefesh HaChaim Shaar 1, Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaMitzvot, Tanya chapters 36–37, Chazal, the Zohar, and the Arizal, this class explains how mitzvot repair the mixture created by the first sin and guide the human being from confusion back to truth.

snippet.title: Why Datan and Aviram Feared Moshe's Words | Datan and Aviram 1 | Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltVDgCK2hQ6DpURicujUN6s

Why do Datan and Aviram keep appearing beside Moshe from Egypt all the way to Korach's rebellion? In part 1 of this English Torah series, Rabbi Eliyahu Bari begins with their first confrontation with Moshe and the strange phrase: "Are you saying to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?"

Watch the full 6-part Datan, Aviram & Korach playlist:
https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltVDgCK2hQ6DpURicujUN6s

This class opens the series by looking at the earliest scene where Chazal identify Datan and Aviram. Moshe sees one Hebrew man striking another, intervenes, and is immediately challenged: "Who made you a man, a prince and a judge over us? Are you saying to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?"

Rashi, following Chazal, reads the word "saying" as a hint that Moshe killed the Egyptian through the Shem HaMeforash, the explicit Divine Name. Gur Aryeh develops why this matters: Datan and Aviram were not simply reporting that Moshe had killed an Egyptian. They recognized that Moshe's power was connected to speech, the Divine Name, and spiritual action.

That recognition should have led to awe and humility. Instead, it became suspicion. They saw holiness, but they interpreted it as danger. They heard Moshe's speech, but instead of hearing redemption, they heard a threat.

The point of the class is not to defend Datan and Aviram. The Torah does not defend them. The question is deeper: what did they recognize in Moshe, and why did they turn that recognition into fear rather than trust?

This first moment becomes the seed of the later conflict. The same pattern returns when Datan and Aviram accuse Moshe in Egypt, refuse to gather the mann, stand with Korach, and speak the language of death and accusation against the very person sent to redeem them.

In this video:
1. Why Chazal identify the two fighting Hebrew men as Datan and Aviram.
2. Why the phrase "Are you saying to kill me" matters.
3. How Rashi explains Moshe's use of the Shem HaMeforash.
4. How Gur Aryeh frames the power of holy speech.
5. Why Datan and Aviram's problem was not ignorance, but distorted spiritual perception.
6. How fear of Moshe's speech becomes a pattern of opposition to redemption.
7. Why this early episode prepares the later rebellion of Korach.

Series roadmap:
Part 1 - Why They Feared Moshe's Speech
Part 2 - When Redemption Looks Like Suffering
Part 3 - The Price of Geulah
Part 4 - How Korach Turned Pain Into Ideology
Part 5 - Why the Torah Proves Moshe Right
Part 6 - The Arizal's Tikkun Through Eliyahu

snippet.title: When Redemption Made Suffering Worse | Datan and Aviram 2 | Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltVDgCK2hQ6DpURicujUN6s

In part 2 of this 6-part English Torah series on Datan, Aviram, and Korach, Rabbi Eliyahu Bari studies one of the most painful early moments in the story of Moshe Rabbeinu’s mission: Moshe goes to Pharaoh in the name of Hashem, and instead of freedom beginning immediately, the slavery becomes worse.

Pharaoh removes the straw, keeps the same quota of bricks, and the officers of Israel confront Moshe and Aharon with a devastating accusation: “May Hashem look upon you and judge, because you have made our smell foul in the eyes of Pharaoh and his servants, to put a sword in their hand to kill us.”

According to Rashi, the people standing against Moshe here are Datan and Aviram. That means this is not an isolated complaint. It continues the pattern that began in part 1: Datan and Aviram recognize that Moshe’s words carry unusual spiritual power, but instead of trusting that holy speech, they experience it as danger.

In the first video, they ask Moshe: “Are you saying to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?” Chazal understand this as a hint to Moshe using the Shem HaMeforash, the explicit Divine Name. In this second video, that fear becomes stronger. Moshe speaks to Pharaoh, and the visible result is more suffering. From their perspective, Moshe’s redemption seems to place a sword in Pharaoh’s hand.

The class does not defend Datan and Aviram. The Torah does not defend them. But it does ask a deeper question: how does a real pain become a wrong accusation? How does a question about suffering become machloket?

Moshe himself asks a version of the same question. At the end of Shemot chapter 5, Moshe turns to Hashem and says: “Why have You done evil to this people? Why did You send me?” Moshe is not ignoring the suffering. He sees it. He feels it. But Moshe brings the question upward, to Hashem. Datan and Aviram take the pain sideways, into accusation against Moshe.

That difference is one of the main lessons of this class. The same pain can become tefillah, or it can become machloket. The same hard question can become humility before Hashem, or it can become rebellion against the messenger Hashem sent.

1. In this video:
1. Why Pharaoh made the slavery worse after Moshe began his mission.
2. How Rashi identifies the opponents in this scene with Datan and Aviram.
3. Why their accusation continues the theme from the first confrontation with Moshe.
4. Why real suffering does not automatically justify rebellion.
5. What separates Moshe’s question to Hashem from Datan and Aviram’s accusation against Moshe.
6. How this scene prepares the later claim that Moshe brought the people out to die.
7. Why this story is essential for understanding the later rebellion of Korach.

2. Main sources discussed:
1. Shemot 5:20-23.
2. Rashi to Shemot 5:20.
3. Moshe’s question to Hashem at the end of Shemot chapter 5.
4. The broader Torah pattern of Datan and Aviram opposing Moshe from Egypt to Korach.

snippet.title: The Price of Redemption in Egypt | Datan and Aviram 3 | Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltVDgCK2hQ6DpURicujUN6s

In part 3 of this 6-part English Torah series on Datan, Aviram, and Korach, Rabbi Eliyahu Bari turns to one of the most difficult Midrashic ideas about Yetziat Mitzrayim: during Makkat Choshech, the plague of darkness, Jews who did not want to leave Egypt died, and only one-fifth of Israel left according to the classic reading of Rashi on “chamushim.”

This class uses that painful background to deepen the story of Datan and Aviram. Their accusation against Moshe is not treated as justified. The Torah does not defend their rebellion. But their words across the Torah show a recurring pattern: they experience Moshe’s mission, Moshe’s speech, and Moshe’s Geulah as dangerous.

In part 1, Datan and Aviram feared Moshe’s holy speech. In part 2, they accused Moshe and Aharon of putting a sword in Pharaoh’s hand when Pharaoh made the slavery worse. In part 3, the question becomes even sharper: how would they understand a redemption that came together with plague, judgment, loss, and painful birur?

Rabbi Eliyahu Bari presents this carefully as a chiddush, not as an explicit statement of Chazal: perhaps Datan and Aviram represent the person who wants Geulah, but not if Geulah demands judgment; not if it separates those who truly want to leave Egypt from those who remain inwardly attached to it; not if redemption requires truth instead of comfort.

This does not make Datan and Aviram right. It makes the rebellion more serious. A person can ask a real question about suffering and still take that question in the wrong direction. Compassion, when detached from humility before Hashem, can become an argument against the very process of redemption.

The larger lesson is not only about Egypt. It is about every time a person wants redemption, growth, or spiritual change, but resists the painful birur that makes it real. Egypt cannot simply be carried into Sinai. Geulah means leaving Egypt outwardly and inwardly.

1. In this video:
1. Rashi on Makkat Choshech and the Jews who did not want to leave Egypt.
2. The Midrashic reading that only one-fifth of Israel left Egypt.
3. Why Datan and Aviram may have struggled with the cost of Geulah.
4. Why their survival during the plague of darkness makes their story more complex.
5. The difference between wanting redemption and accepting the birur of redemption.
6. Why pain over Jewish loss must not become rebellion against Hashem’s process.
7. How this prepares the later accusation that Moshe brought the people out to die.

2. Main sources discussed:
1. Rashi to Shemot 10:22.
2. Rashi to Shemot 13:18.
3. The Midrashic tradition about those who did not want to leave Egypt dying during darkness.
4. The broader Torah pattern of Datan and Aviram speaking about Moshe’s mission as a path toward death.

snippet.title: When Korach Turned Pain Into Rebellion | Datan and Aviram 4 | Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltVDgCK2hQ6DpURicujUN6s

In part 4 of this 6-part English Torah series on Datan, Aviram, and Korach, Rabbi Eliyahu Bari shows why Korach became the perfect partner for Datan and Aviram. They were not making exactly the same argument, but together they created one of the most dangerous rebellions in the Torah.

Datan and Aviram speak in the language of history and pain: Moshe brought us out of Egypt to die in the desert. Korach speaks in the language of holiness and ideology: “The whole congregation, all of them, are holy, and Hashem is among them. Why do you raise yourselves over the congregation of Hashem?”

That combination is powerful. Datan and Aviram bring the emotional fuel: a painful Geulah, a fear that Moshe’s mission leads to death, and resentment over the cost of redemption. Korach gives that pain a religious argument: if everyone is holy, why Moshe, why Aharon, why Kehunah, why hierarchy?

The class explains why this is so spiritually dangerous. Korach says something that sounds true. All Israel is holy. The pain of Datan and Aviram also contains something real: Jewish suffering is not something to dismiss. But a true sentence can become false when it is used against Hashem’s will.

Rabbi Eliyahu Bari also brings the Zohar’s deeper frame. In the Zohar on Korach, machloket is not merely a disagreement. It is separation above and below. Aharon represents the right side, Chesed. The Levi’im are connected to the left side, Gevurah. Korach wants the left to take the place of the right instead of being sweetened and ordered properly.

This gives a deeper way to understand the rebellion. It is not only politics. It is not only personality. It is a breakdown of Shalom. And since the Holy Name is called Shalom, machloket becomes a fight against the very unity that holiness is supposed to reveal.

The key lesson: holy language is not automatically holy when it is used for division. Compassion, equality, concern for the people, and the claim that everyone is holy can all be real values. But when they are used to attack the Divine order, they become tools of rebellion.

6. Chesed, Gevurah, Aharon, Levi’im, and the spiritual structure of Korach’s rebellion.
7. Why holy language must be joined to humility, Shalom, and submission to Hashem.

snippet.title: How the Torah Proves Moshe Was Right | Datan and Aviram 5 | Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltVDgCK2hQ6DpURicujUN6s

In part 5 of this 6-part English Torah series on Datan, Aviram, and Korach, Rabbi Eliyahu Bari gives the necessary balance to the entire discussion. A serious Torah class can make Datan, Aviram, and Korach psychologically and spiritually interesting, but it must not accidentally give their rebellion a platform.

The Torah is clear: Moshe is right. Aharon is right. Korach, Datan, and Aviram are wrong. The question is how the Torah proves that.

First, Moshe did not appoint himself. At the burning bush, Hashem says that He has seen the suffering of His people, heard their cry, and come down to save them. Moshe’s mission begins with Hashem, not with personal ambition.

Second, the Geulah was announced from the beginning as coming with “great judgments.” The harshness of the process is not Moshe’s failure. Yetziat Mitzrayim is not only an escape from slavery; it is also a birur, a revelation of who truly wants to leave Egypt and move toward Sinai.

Third, Moshe also asks hard questions. At the end of Shemot chapter 5, Moshe says to Hashem: “Why have You done evil to this people? Why did You send me?” Moshe sees the pain. He does not ignore it. But he brings the question upward to Hashem. Datan and Aviram take pain sideways, into accusation and machloket.

Fourth, Moshe has no personal agenda. The Torah testifies that Moshe is exceedingly humble, more than any person on the face of the earth. In the Korach story, Moshe says “lo milibi” - this is not from my own heart. He is not building his own power. He is carrying the mission Hashem gave him.

Fifth, Aharon’s role is confirmed by Hashem. After the rebellion, Aharon’s staff blossoms. Kehunah is not nepotism. It is not Moshe giving honor to his brother. It is Divine life flowing through the vessel Hashem chose.

This class answers the strongest version of the rebels’ argument. Korach is right that all Israel is holy, but wrong that holiness erases structure. Datan and Aviram may feel real pain, but they are wrong to use that pain against Hashem’s process. Kedushah belongs to the whole nation, but it still needs order, humility, and vessels.

The key lesson is sharp: a hard question is not automatically rebellion. Moshe also asks. But a question must be brought with humility before Hashem, not used as a weapon against the messenger Hashem sent.

1. In this video:
1. Why Moshe’s mission begins with Hashem, not with Moshe’s ambition.
2. Why Geulah was announced as judgment and birur.
3. How Moshe asks hard questions without becoming a rebel.
4. What “lo milibi” teaches about Moshe’s humility and authority.
5. Why Aharon’s staff proves the legitimacy of Kehunah.
6. Why Korach’s claim that everyone is holy does not erase Divine structure.
7. Why pain must be brought to Hashem instead of turned into machloket.

snippet.title: The Arizal on Datan and Aviram's Tikkun Through Eliyahu | Part 6 | Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IltVDgCK2hQ6DpURicujUN6s

In part 6, the conclusion of this 6-part English Torah series on Datan, Aviram, and Korach, Rabbi Eliyahu Bari turns to the Arizal’s astonishing teaching: the story of Datan and Aviram does not simply end when the earth swallows them in the rebellion of Korach.

According to the Arizal, their spiritual root appears later in the story of Eliyahu HaNavi at Har Carmel, one of the greatest public revelations of Hashem in Tanach. This final class shows how even the distorted force that opposed Moshe can eventually be redirected into Kiddush Hashem.

The Arizal places Korach, Datan, and Aviram in shoresh Kayin, the spiritual root of Kayin. This root is connected with powerful Gevurah, enormous spiritual force, and real danger when that force is not sweetened. That already changes the way we understand them. They are not random troublemakers. They are spiritually charged souls whose power becomes destructive when it is detached from humility, Shalom, and submission to Hashem.

In Sefer HaLikutim on Parashat Korach, the Arizal connects Datan and Aviram to the two bulls of Eliyahu at Har Carmel. One bull is chosen for Hashem, and the other is chosen for Baal. The Arizal explains that Datan was more sweetened, while Aviram was harsher. Yet even the bull assigned to Baal ultimately becomes part of the revelation of Hashem’s Name.

That is the depth of the tikkun. In the Korach story, Datan and Aviram stand against Moshe and become part of machloket. In the Eliyahu story, their root is forced back into Kiddush Hashem. Even the side that externally appears connected to Baal becomes part of the declaration: Hashem Hu HaElokim.

This does not mean Datan and Aviram were secretly right. They were not. The Torah condemns their rebellion. But the Arizal teaches us not to flatten them into simple villains. Their force was real. Their potential was real. Their corruption was real. And their eventual tikkun is real.

The final lesson of the series is that holy potential must be sweetened. Gevurah without humility becomes accusation. Pain without submission becomes machloket. Spiritual power without Shalom becomes rebellion. But when that same force is brought back to Hashem, it can become part of Kiddush Hashem.

1. In this video:
1. The Arizal’s teaching that Datan and Aviram belong to shoresh Kayin.
2. Why Korach, Datan, and Aviram share a powerful Gevurah root.
3. The two bulls of Eliyahu at Har Carmel and their connection to Datan and Aviram.
4. Why Datan is described as more sweetened and Aviram as harsher.
5. How even the bull connected to Baal becomes part of Kiddush Hashem.
6. Why this tikkun does not justify the rebellion, but deepens our understanding of it.
7. The final life lesson: questions, pain, and spiritual force must be sweetened by humility, Shalom, and service of Hashem.

2. Main sources discussed:
1. Shaar HaGilgulim, Hakdamah 36.
2. Sefer HaLikutim, Parashat Korach.
3. The story of Eliyahu HaNavi at Har Carmel.
4. The declaration “Hashem Hu HaElokim.”
5. The broader connection between Gevurah, machloket, tikkun, and Kiddush Hashem.

snippet.title: Why Do We Say Psalm 27 in Elul? The Secret of the 13 Names – Rabbi Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IlunNMtXWK9Q2pyGw6iqI_47

Why, for the entire month of Elul, twice a day, do we say the same psalm — L'David Hashem Ori (Psalm 27)? The custom is not in the Gemara. It is not in the Rishonim. It is not in the Rambam or the Tur. It appears relatively late — cited in the Shaarei Teshuvah and the Mateh Efrayim, and spread through the siddurim from there. The Vilna Gaon did not say it at all. And yet within a few generations it became one of the most universally kept customs of the Jewish year: Chassidim say it, Litvaks say it, Sefardim say it. This class asks what exactly caught — and answers it in four layers, from pshat through remez and Kabbalah to Chassidus.

Watch both language versions of this lesson:
Russian version: https://youtube.com/watch?v=gm-AfoXyO9s

PSHAT. We begin with the Midrash. The Midrash Shocher Tov, echoed in Vayikra Rabbah, reads the opening verse as a map of the entire season: "Ori" — my light — is Rosh Hashanah, the day the world is lit by judgment; "v'yishi" — my salvation — is Yom Kippur; "ki yitzpeneini b'suko" — He will hide me in His shelter — is Sukkos. The whole season folded into a single pasuk. Hence the timing: from Rosh Chodesh Elul, when the season begins, the psalm begins.

But that explains the timing, not the choice. Why this psalm? It is a psalm about siege — "if an army encamps against me," "for my father and my mother have abandoned me." There are psalms about teshuvah; there is Psalm 51, the great confession. Why give Elul a psalm about fear? The answer we develop reframes the whole mizmor: Elul is honest about what we would rather not say out loud. It asks us to look at the year that just ended — at who we promised we would be, and who we turned out to be. The psalm names that fear directly, but it names it in the second half of the verse. The first half is light: "Hashem ori v'yishi" — and only then "mimi ira." The light comes first.

REMEZ. The word "lulei" — "had I not believed I would see the goodness of Hashem" — is the letters of "Elul" rearranged, and both equal 67. And more importantly: the Shem Havayah appears in this psalm thirteen times, corresponding to the Yud-Gimmel Middos HaRachamim, the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy that form the entire spiritual architecture of the month.

KABBALAH. The Arizal teaches that Elul is when the Yud-Gimmel Tikkunei Dikna — the thirteen attributes of mercy at their very root — shine downward into our world. These are the forty days that began when Moshe ascended Har Sinai a third time on Rosh Chodesh Elul for the second luchos, and ended on Yom Kippur with "salachti kidvarecha." The hint sits in the verse everyone knows: "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li" — the first letters spell Elul, and the four final letters (yud × 4) give forty, the forty days themselves.

CHASSIDUS. The Alter Rebbe, in Likkutei Torah, gives the mashal that has become the defining image of Elul: all year the King is in His palace, where you need an appointment and standing to enter, but once a year He goes out into the field, and there anyone who wishes may approach and is received with a smiling face. Melech ba'sadeh. And then you hear that the psalm is not written from outside the gates but by someone already let close: "Achas sha'alti" — one thing I ask. Not a list. Not "rescue me," but "shivti b'veis Hashem kol yemei chayai" — presence, not outcome. And the line "Lecha amar libi bakshu fanai": the summons came from inside, not outside — what Chassidus calls penimiyus haratzon, the innermost will, which does not need to be created in Elul but heard.

The class closes on the doubled "kavei el Hashem" at the end of the psalm and the Gemara's answer in Berachos 32b: if a person davened and was not answered, let him daven again.

--- IN THIS CLASS ---

Where the custom of L'David Hashem Ori comes from, and why the Vilna Gaon did not have it

The Midrash that folds Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkos into one verse

Why Elul was given a psalm about fear rather than a psalm about repentance

The thirteen Names in the psalm and the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy

The Arizal: Moshe's forty days as a channel that reopens every year

The Alter Rebbe: the King in the field — and what the mashal changes in the psalm

--- SOURCES ---

Tell me in the comments which psalm or commentary you would like me to take apart next. It helps spread Torah learning and makes this channel stronger.

snippet.title: One Cup, Many Cups: The Kabbalistic Secret of Kiddush - Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:

▶ WATCH MORE SHABBAT AND KIDDUSH TEACHINGS:

Why do we share the Kiddush wine at the Shabbat table? 

What appears to be a simple Jewish custom opens the door to a profound connection between Halachah, Kabbalah, Moshe Rabbeinu, the seventy elders, and the spiritual meaning of true leadership. 

In this Torah class, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the deeper meaning of the Kos Shel Berachah — the cup of blessing. 

One person makes Kiddush, yet the blessing is meant to reach everyone. 

One cup becomes the source. 

Many cups become vessels to receive. 

On the halachic level, we explore why everyone present should ideally taste from the Kiddush wine, as well as the important concept of pagum wine. 

Then we enter the Kabbalistic dimension. 

The Kiddush cup can be understood as a kli — a vessel for spiritual blessing. Wine represents a powerful spiritual flow and is associated with Gevurah — strength, intensity, and judgment. Through Kiddush, that intensity is elevated and sweetened. 

But the blessing does not remain in one vessel. 

It flows outward. 

This becomes a powerful parallel to the story of Moshe Rabbeinu and the seventy elders in Parshat Beha’alotcha. 

Hashem tells Moshe that He will take from the ruach resting upon Moshe and place it upon the elders. 

Does Moshe lose anything when others receive from his ruach? 

No. 

Chazal compare Moshe to a candle used to light many other candles. The original flame is not diminished because its light has been shared. 

This reveals a fundamental principle of spiritual life: 

One source. Many receivers. 
One flame. Many flames. 
One Kiddush cup. Many cups. 
One blessing. Many participants. 

The teachings of the Arizal, transmitted by Rabbi Chaim Vital in Shaar HaGilgulim, deepen this idea through the concepts of higher ruach, spiritual refinement, and ibur — the assistance that souls of tzaddikim can provide in a person’s service of Hashem. 

The result is a profound lesson not only about Kiddush, but about Jewish leadership, parenting, teaching, and spiritual transmission. 

A true leader does not keep the light for himself. 

A parent cannot be the only spiritual vessel in the home. 

A rabbi cannot be the only vessel in the community. 

A teacher cannot be the only cup. 

Each person must become a vessel. 

And eventually, the receiver must become a source for someone else. 

That is the deeper message of the Shabbat table: 

Kedushah is not weakened when it is shared. 
It becomes complete when it spreads.

snippet.title: Rosh Hashanah: The Secret of Dormita and Spiritual Sleep | Arizal | 1 of 5 | Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:

Russian version of this lesson:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EAmMMvFQUTQ

Watch the complete five-part series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLKTLsA4MaNkc

This is Lesson 1 of 5. Continue to Lesson 2, “Nesirah: Why Separation Is Necessary for Unity,” in the playlist.

Why does Rosh Hashanah—the day of awakening and the sounding of the shofar—begin, according to the Arizal, with a profound state of spiritual sleep? 

In Video 1 of our five-part series “Arizal on Rosh Hashanah,” we explore one of the most fascinating teachings recorded by Rabbi Chaim Vital in Sha’ar HaKavanot: דורמיטא — Dormita. 

The Arizal connects what happens on Rosh Hashanah to the creation of Adam HaRishon. The Torah tells us: 

וַיַּפֵּל ה׳ אֱלֹהִים תַּרְדֵּמָה עַל הָאָדָם וַיִּישָׁן 

“And Hashem God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept.” 

First comes sleep. Then separation. Then building. Eventually Adam and Chava can encounter one another as two distinct beings. 

According to the Arizal, this primordial process becomes a model for the spiritual transformation of Rosh Hashanah. 

In this class, we introduce Zeir Anpin and Nukva and examine their initial state of אחור באחור — achor be-achor, “back-to-back.” Before they can ultimately reach פנים בפנים — panim be-panim, “face-to-face,” a profound restructuring must take place. 

That process begins with Dormita. 

We explore what the Arizal means when he describes the withdrawal of the Mochin, why spiritual consciousness must undergo a temporary withdrawal, and why rebuilding can sometimes begin not with an increase of light, but with its concealment. 

This also opens a deeper perspective on Rosh Hashanah as Yom HaDin — the Day of Judgment. 

Judgment is not presented only as a Divine response to human actions. Within the Arizal’s description of Rosh Hashanah, the Dinim also participate in a process of spiritual differentiation and construction. Limitation creates definition. Separation makes a new kind of relationship possible. 

Rosh Hashanah therefore becomes much more than simply changing the date from one year to another. The spiritual configuration itself undergoes a process of renewal: 

Dormita → Nesirah → rebuilding → awakening → panim be-panim. 

And this leads to an extraordinary question. 

If Zeir Anpin enters Dormita and the Mochin withdraw, what causes the awakening? 

The answer leads directly to the central mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah: the shofar. 

According to the Arizal, the shofar does far more than awaken the human heart to teshuvah. Its sound participates in the spiritual process of awakening and the renewed drawing of Mochin. 

But before we can fully understand the shofar, we first need to understand why the separation was necessary. 

That mysterious process is called נסירה — Nesirah. 

In Video 2, we will explore why Zeir Anpin and Nukva must move from achor be-achor toward panim be-panim, why separation is necessary before a true face-to-face relationship can emerge, and what all of this has to do with the Dinim of Rosh Hashanah.
