snippet.title: Ор аХаим Трума 2/2 – Ковчег Завета: личная или общая миссия? – Рав Элиягу Бари
snippet.description:
Смотрите всю серию по порядку:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IlsKtWQBhDlIn_JR2W_bBXCt

Почему при заповеди о строительстве Ковчега Завета Тора неожиданно говорит во множественном числе: «И сделают ковчег» (ועשו ארון), тогда как в отношении Мишкана, жертвенника, стола и меноры используется форма единственного числа — «и сделай» (ועשית)? Почему именно Арону — центральному символу Торы — приписана такая необычная грамматическая форма? В этом глубоком уроке по комментарию Ор аХаим Рав Элиягу Бари раскрывает фундаментальный принцип коллективной ответственности за Тору и объясняет скрытую структуру текста. 

На первый взгляд перед нами всего лишь грамматическая особенность. Однако Ор аХаим учит: в Торе нет случайных формулировок. Если Тора меняет форму обращения с единственного числа на множественное, значит, здесь заложено особое послание. Все указания о строительстве Мишкана даны Моше в форме «ты сделаешь». И вдруг — «они сделают ковчег». Более того, далее, при описании деталей, текст снова возвращается к форме единственного числа: «и покрой его чистым золотом». Почему такая смена? 

Первое объяснение связано с самой сутью Торы. Ковчег — это не просто предмет Святилища. Он содержит Скрижали Завета, символизирует саму Тору. Ор аХаим предлагает увидеть здесь намёк: Тора не может быть исполнена одним человеком. Ни один еврей, каким бы праведным он ни был, не способен выполнить все заповеди. Коэн не может выполнить заповеди, относящиеся к простому израильтянину, например, отделение даров для коэна или выкуп первенца сына. Левит также ограничен своей ролью. Израильтянин не может исполнять храмовую службу коэна. Таким образом, полнота исполнения Торы возможна только через весь народ Израиля как единое целое. Поэтому о Ковчеге сказано во множественном числе — «и сделают»: Тора принадлежит всем и строится усилиями всех. 

Второе объяснение Ор аХаим видит в том, что множественное число служит вступлением ко всему проекту строительства Мишкана. Даже если далее используется форма единственного числа, это не означает, что Моше действовал в одиночку. Он представлял всех «хахмей лев» — мудрых сердцем мастеров, которые участвовали в строительстве. Единственное число указывает на руководство, но множественное — на коллективную реализацию. Грамматика подчёркивает структуру лидерства и участия народа. 

Третье объяснение связано с существованием двух ковчегов. До получения вторых Скрижалей Моше по указанию Всевышнего изготовил временный деревянный ковчег (Дварим 10:1–5), чтобы поместить туда Скрижали сразу после спуска с горы Синай. Там сказано в единственном числе: «сделай себе ковчег». Этот ковчег был временным и, по мнению комментаторов, изготовленным лично Моше. В нашем разделе речь идёт о другом, постоянном Ковчеге, который должен был быть построен Бецалелем и мастерами для Мишкана. Если бы Тора снова использовала форму «и сделай», можно было бы подумать, что речь идёт о том же ковчеге или что он должен быть построен лично Моше за его счёт. Чтобы избежать недоразумений, Тора использует форму «и сделают», ясно указывая на новый, общественный проект. 

Таким образом, грамматическая деталь раскрывает три уровня понимания: коллективную природу исполнения Торы, структуру лидерства в строительстве Мишкана и различие между временным и постоянным Ковчегом. Ор аХаим показывает, как одно слово способно изменить наше восприятие всей системы заповедей. 

Сегодня этот урок имеет особую актуальность. В эпоху индивидуализма Тора напоминает: духовное совершенство достигается не изоляцией, а принадлежностью к общине. Нельзя построить «ковчег Торы» в одиночку. Каждая душа вносит свою часть в общую святость. Только вместе народ Израиля становится носителем Божественного присутствия.

Практический урок о роли каждого в общем служении

snippet.title: Black Hole Cosmology & Tzimtzum 1/4 – Intro – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IluxxOqJUCNHI-Vj3V6VpciE

What if modern astrophysics is rediscovering what Kabbalah described centuries ago? Could spinning black holes and the cosmic axis of the universe reflect the mystical doctrine of Tzimtzum — the Divine contraction that made creation possible?

In this profound and thought-provoking lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the fascinating parallels between rotating black holes, cosmic spin, and the Lurianic concept of Tzimtzum as taught by Rabbi Isaac Luria, the Arizal. Modern physics suggests that our universe may exist inside a spinning black hole, inheriting a preferred axis of rotation from a “parent universe.” Meanwhile, Kabbalah teaches that before creation, the Infinite Light (Ohr Ein Sof) filled all reality until a Divine contraction concealed that light, forming a metaphysical void where creation could unfold.

Astrophysical discoveries — including surprising evidence that galaxies may share a common rotational direction — challenge the assumption of a random universe. If the cosmos has a preferred axis, what does that imply? Physicist Nikodem Popławski’s black hole cosmology proposes that every black hole could generate a new expanding universe beyond its event horizon. In this model, gravitational collapse becomes a cosmic womb, and rotation becomes inherited structure.

Remarkably, this scientific narrative echoes the Kabbalistic structure of Tzimtzum. First, contraction and concealment. Then, a measured re-emanation of light through the kav — a single Divine ray entering the void. Just as a spinning black hole traps most light but emits focused jets and gravitational waves, so too Tzimtzum withholds infinite illumination while allowing a controlled revelation sufficient for finite worlds to exist.

We examine deep structural parallels:
• Singularity and Divine contraction
• Event horizon and concealed void
• Cosmic spin and the kav’s directional flow
• Gravitational waves and the mystical reshimu (imprint)
• Big Bounce cosmology and emanation of the Sefirot

Black hole mergers generate ripples in spacetime — echoes from hidden realms. In Kabbalistic thought, concealment is never absolute; even within the void remains a trace of Divine presence. Could gravitational waves be physical metaphors for spiritual reverberations? Could cosmic rotation be the physical imprint of a higher frame of reference?

This lecture does not attempt to reduce mysticism to physics or physics to mysticism. Instead, it highlights philosophical resonance. Both systems confront the same ultimate mystery: how does something emerge from apparent nothingness? In Kabbalah, creation begins with hiddenness. In cosmology, the universe emerges from a singularity or perhaps from within a black hole beyond observable space.

Rotation plays a central role in both frameworks. If the universe rotates, it rotates relative to something greater. In Tzimtzum, the finite world exists within the Infinite, even if that Infinity is concealed. Cosmic spin becomes a powerful metaphor for Divine will — an axis that silently organizes existence.

Through clear explanations and accessible metaphors, Rav Eliyahu Bari connects black hole cosmology, Einstein-Cartan gravity, galaxy alignment observations, and Lurianic Kabbalah into a unified exploration of creation, concealment, and emergence.

snippet.title: Black Holes and Kabbalah: The Arizal’s Tzimtzum and Modern Cosmology
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3IluxxOqJUCNHI-Vj3V6VpciE

Did our universe begin inside a spinning black hole? 

Modern astrophysics is exploring a bold possibility: that our universe may have been born inside a rotating black hole in a larger cosmos. At the same time, the Arizal (Rabbi Isaac Luria) teaches that creation began with Tzimtzum — a Divine concealment of Infinite Light, followed by a measured re-entry of light into a hidden space. 

Are these two ideas connected? 

In this lecture, we explore the structural parallels between black hole cosmology and the Kabbalistic concept of Tzimtzum. This is not an attempt to force Torah into physics or physics into Torah. Rather, it is a comparison of patterns — contraction, concealment, emergence, and structure. 

Recent astronomical observations have suggested something surprising: many galaxies appear to rotate in the same direction. If confirmed, this challenges the idea that the universe is completely random and isotropic. Some physicists, including Nikodem Popławski, argue that if the universe has an overall spin, it may have inherited that rotation from something larger — possibly a spinning black hole in a “parent” universe. 

In black hole cosmology, a massive star collapses into a black hole. Instead of ending in a final singularity, some models propose that the collapse “bounces” and expands from within, appearing as a Big Bang from the inside. In that case, every black hole could potentially give birth to a new universe. 

Now compare that to the Arizal’s teaching: 

Before creation, there was only Ein Sof — Infinite Divine Light. In order for finite reality to exist, Hashem performed Tzimtzum — concealing His infinite presence and creating a “space” (chalal panui) where creation could unfold. After the concealment, a thin ray of light — the kav — entered that space and began building structure through the Sefirot and the worlds. 

The structure is striking: 

• Contraction before expansion 
• Hidden interior before revelation 
• Darkness before light 
• Limited, measured emergence 
• Orientation and direction 

Black holes trap nearly all light — yet sometimes powerful jets burst outward. When black holes merge, they emit gravitational waves — ripples in spacetime that scientists detected for the first time in 2015. We did not see the collision. We heard it. 

Even in total darkness, something emerges. 

In Kabbalah, Tzimtzum does not mean absence — it means concealment. A reshimu, a trace, remains. The Infinite is hidden, not gone. 

Both frameworks suggest that what appears to be destruction may actually be preparation. What looks like emptiness may be the beginning of structure. What feels like darkness may be the womb of light. 

This lecture covers: 

– Black hole formation and rotation 
– The possibility of a spinning universe 
– Universe inside a black hole theory 
– Tzimtzum explained clearly 
– The kav and Divine structure 
– Concealment as creative force 
– Gravitational waves as echoes from hidden realms 
– Philosophical implications for faith and science 

Is this proof of anything? No. 

But it reveals something powerful: 

Both science and Kabbalah describe a reality where creation begins with contraction. 

Not explosion first — but concealment first. 

Before revelation, there is hiddenness. 
Before light, there is darkness. 
Before expansion, there is inward collapse. 

And that pattern may not only explain the cosmos. 

It may explain our lives. 

If you found this lecture meaningful, please like, share, and subscribe for more Torah and science discussions.

snippet.title: Quantum Physics in Pirkei Avot 1/8 – Ethics of Our Fathers – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3Ilu1xDuxglADoBPJjUVq74Vx

What if modern quantum physics is uncovering the very same truth that the Torah revealed thousands of years ago? What if the “Heavenly Ledger” described by our Sages is not just a moral metaphor—but the literal architecture of reality itself? 

In this groundbreaking lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the astonishing convergence between Torah wisdom and cutting-edge science. For generations, we have learned the powerful words from Pirkei Avot: “An eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds are written in a book.” We were taught that the ledger is open and the hand writes. These teachings shaped our understanding of Hashgacha Pratit, Divine Providence, and personal responsibility. But what if these statements are not poetic symbolism? What if they describe the fundamental structure of the universe? 

This class dives deep into one of the most perplexing problems in theoretical physics: the Black Hole Information Paradox. Modern physicists struggle with a central question in quantum mechanics—can information ever truly be destroyed? The emerging scientific consensus is extraordinary: information is never lost. Even when matter disappears into a black hole, the information encoded within it remains preserved on the event horizon. The universe itself appears to function like a perfect, indestructible recording system. 

Now consider the Torah perspective. From the Zohar to Lurianic Kabbalah, from the Maharal of Prague to the Baal Shem Tov, Jewish mystical tradition has long described reality as layered with spiritual imprint and permanent trace. The concept of Reshimu teaches that every spiritual action leaves an eternal mark. Every thought, every word, every deed creates a lasting imprint in the cosmic structure. The world is not a temporary stage—it is a dynamic recording field. 

In this lecture, we carefully examine how the quantum principle of information conservation mirrors the Torah’s teaching that nothing is ever erased. We explore how the “Book of Remembrance” described by our Sages aligns conceptually with the idea that the boundary of a black hole stores encoded information. We analyze how the Neshama, the eternal soul, functions within a universe that never deletes data. And we discuss how Techiyat HaMetim—the Resurrection of the Dead—can be understood through the lens of ultimate information recovery. 

This is not a superficial comparison between science and religion. It is a deep, disciplined exploration of how Torah and quantum physics may be describing the same underlying system from different languages. The Black Hole Information Paradox becomes more than a physics puzzle—it becomes a window into Divine Providence. Hashgacha is no longer abstract; it is woven into the quantum fabric of existence. 

For serious students of Torah, this class offers a powerful strengthening of emunah grounded in intellectual rigor. For seekers of science, it presents a framework in which faith and physics are not enemies but partners in truth. The Eternal Torah Record is not mythology—it may be the operating system of creation. 

If quantum mechanics teaches that no information can ever be destroyed, then every human action carries infinite weight. Every struggle, every hidden act of integrity, every quiet moment of growth is permanently encoded into reality. Nothing vanishes. Nothing is forgotten. The ledger is open.

snippet.title: Quantum Physics in Pirkei Avot 2/8 – Ethics of Our Fathers – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLDKe3hTC3Ilu1xDuxglADoBPJjUVq74Vx

Is the universe slowly erasing you—or is it recording you with absolute precision? What if the deepest fear of humanity—that our lives fade into nothing—is directly contradicted by both quantum physics and the Eternal Torah? 

In this second installment of The Quantum Ledger series, Rav Eliyahu Bari takes us into the heart of a revolutionary convergence between modern science and ancient Jewish wisdom. Humanity has always struggled with the anxiety that time is a destroyer, that memory fades, and that identity dissolves into the past. If nothing leaves a permanent trace, morality becomes fragile. Justice becomes uncertain. Meaning becomes negotiable. 

The Torah responded to this fear thousands of years ago with a radical declaration: “All your deeds are written in a book.” This is not merely poetic imagery. It is a theological assertion that reality itself contains a perfect moral accounting. Every action, every intention, every exertion of will is permanently inscribed within the structure of existence. The “Sefer,” the Heavenly Book, represents a dimension of reality that cannot be corrupted or erased. 

Meanwhile, modern physics arrived at a strikingly similar conclusion—but through equations instead of prophecy. In quantum mechanics, one of the most fundamental principles is Unitarity. This law states that the evolution of a quantum system is fully reversible. Probabilities are conserved. The total information describing a system can never vanish. If one had perfect access to the universe’s data, one could theoretically rewind events to their precise origin. 

Physicists even formalized this idea through what is known as the No-Hiding Theorem. This theorem demonstrates that information cannot be destroyed and cannot be completely concealed. It can be scrambled, redistributed, encoded in different forms—but it can never be eliminated. The universe, at its most basic level, refuses to delete data. 

Here we encounter a profound alignment with Torah thought. When the Sages spoke about a “Pinkas,” a Ledger, they were not describing a physical notebook in the sky. They were revealing that reality itself contains a hidden dimension of exact accounting. Jewish mystical tradition describes existence as layered with spiritual imprint. Every choice produces consequence not only in the visible world, but in the informational fabric of creation. 

This is where the concept of Da’at Elyon—Supernal Knowledge—becomes transformative. God does not “remember” the way humans remember. Memory implies time, and the Creator stands beyond time. Instead, existence itself persists because it is known. Divine Providence, Hashgacha, is not surveillance. It is an active, continuous feedback loop between human free will and the eternal informational structure of reality. 

When quantum physics declares that information is never lost, and the Torah declares that every deed is eternally written, we are forced to reconsider the nature of accountability. Morality is not sustained by social agreement alone. It is built into the operating system of the cosmos. The universe is not morally neutral. It is informationally exact. 

This lecture carefully bridges scientific rigor with Torah depth. We break down Unitarity in accessible language. We explain how conservation of information reshapes our understanding of physical law. Then we map these principles onto the Torah’s description of the Eternal Ledger. The convergence is not superficial—it is structural. Two radically different intellectual traditions are pointing toward the same conclusion: nothing you do disappears. 

And this leads to the inevitable question: what happens when something appears to be destroyed? What about the most violent, extreme objects in existence—black holes? If anything in the universe could erase information, it would be them. Yet modern physics has discovered something astonishing. 

In the next part of this series, we will confront the Black Hole Information Paradox and see how a crisis in physics forced scientists to reaffirm the very principle the Torah has always taught: reality does not forget.

Can even a black hole erase reality—or does the universe protect every fragment of information forever? What if the most destructive forces in existence actually prove the Torah’s teaching that the soul and its actions are indestructible? 

In this powerful continuation of The Quantum Ledger series, Rav Eliyahu Bari takes us into the heart of one of the greatest crises in modern physics: the Black Hole Information Paradox. We begin with a simple but unsettling image. Imagine burning an entire library to ash. Intuitively, we assume the knowledge is gone forever. Yet quantum mechanics insists otherwise. If one could gather every particle of smoke and every atom of residue, the original information could, in principle, be reconstructed. Information is never lost. 

Then came the challenge. In the 1970s, the study of black holes shook this foundational rule. According to Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity, a black hole possesses gravity so intense that nothing—not even light—can escape once it crosses the Event Horizon. For decades, scientists believed anything passing that boundary was permanently cut off from the universe. 

But Stephen Hawking introduced a revolutionary discovery: black holes emit radiation and slowly evaporate. Over unimaginable spans of time, they disappear. This triggered a scientific earthquake. If a black hole swallows information and then evaporates into random thermal radiation, it would seem that the information is destroyed. The universe’s “rewind button,” guaranteed by quantum mechanics, would be broken. The cosmic ledger would fail. 

This tension became known as the Black Hole Information Paradox. For a moment in scientific history, it appeared that the universe might truly forget. 

Yet physics did not surrender. Through decades of intense debate and mathematical development, researchers arrived at a breathtaking insight: the Holographic Principle. Rather than being lost inside the black hole’s singularity, the information of any object that falls inward becomes encoded on the two-dimensional surface of the black hole—the Event Horizon itself. The surface acts as a storage boundary. Every interaction leaves a precise informational imprint. 

In other words, the black hole does not destroy the data. It records it. 

Further developments, including calculations known as the Page Curve, demonstrated that as a black hole evaporates, the information is not erased. It slowly leaks back into the universe in an extraordinarily complex and encrypted form. The cosmos preserves its files. Even the most violent gravitational collapse cannot delete information; it can only transform and conceal it. 

Now pause and consider the Torah perspective. In Pirkei Avot, our Sages teach that “all your deeds are written in a book.” This is not a metaphor about ink and parchment. It is a description of system architecture. Reality itself contains a recording surface. The Heavenly Ledger is not a poetic exaggeration—it is the spiritual analogue of the informational boundary physicists discovered at the edge of black holes. 

Jewish thought has always maintained that the Neshama, the soul, is indestructible. Actions performed in this world generate permanent spiritual impact. Nothing meaningful vanishes. Just as the Event Horizon preserves physical information, the spiritual structure of creation preserves moral information. The universe is not morally indifferent; it is morally encoded. 

In this lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari carefully connects the Black Hole Information Paradox, the Holographic Principle, and the Page Curve with Torah teachings about accountability, eternity, and the indestructible soul. The convergence is not superficial. Both physics and Torah insist on the same radical truth: annihilation is an illusion. Transformation is real. Encryption is real. But deletion is not. 

This realization changes everything. If even a black hole cannot erase information, then no act of kindness, no hidden sacrifice, no private struggle is ever lost. The cosmic ledger is not fragile. It is built into the deepest laws of existence. 

In our next session, we will open the precise words of Pirkei Avot and explore the teachings of the Maharal of Prague to understand how our choices become the “pen” that writes onto the fabric of reality itself. 

--- IN THIS VIDEO ---

How the Holographic Principle shows information is encoded on the Event Horizon 

What this reveals about the eternity of the Neshama and human accountability 

If this lecture deepened your understanding of Torah and modern science, like this video, subscribe for the next installment, and share it with someone seeking clarity about faith and physics.

snippet.title: Quantum Physics in Pirkei Avot 4/8 – Ethics of Our Fathers – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
famous teaching from Pirkei Avot is not describing surveillance, but system design? 

In this third installment of The Quantum Ledger series, Rav Eliyahu Bari reveals a revolutionary way to understand one of the most well-known teachings in Torah: “Know what is above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds are written in a book.” For generations, this statement has been heard as a warning—a cosmic security camera reminding us to behave. But when examined through deep Hasidic thought and modern quantum physics, the meaning becomes far more profound. 

The Maggid of Mezritch offered a startling reinterpretation of the Hebrew phrase “Da ma lema’alah mimach.” It can also mean: “Know that what is above is from you.” The higher worlds are not passive observers. They are reactive systems. Spiritual reality is not static—it responds. The “Eye that sees” is not merely watching; it is waiting. 

This concept mirrors one of the most astonishing principles in quantum mechanics: the Observer Effect. In quantum theory, particles exist in a superposition of possibilities until an interaction forces them to collapse into a definite state. Reality, at its deepest level, is not fixed until it is engaged. Observation is not passive; it is participatory. 

Torah thought suggests something remarkably similar. The upper worlds remain in potential until human free will activates them. Your choices are not small, isolated gestures. They are triggers within a vast spiritual mechanism. The universe is wired to respond. 

But what about the “Book”? If the Creator is beyond time and possesses complete knowledge, why would there be any need for writing? The Maharal of Prague addressed this question directly. The Book is not a reminder for God. It is the dimension of reality where fleeting physical actions become permanent existence. 

Every action you perform in the physical world is momentary. It happens and seems to disappear. But the will, intention, and energy behind it do not vanish. Just as spoken words fade unless written down, the “Book” represents the mechanism through which actions are stabilized into enduring reality. It is the cosmological surface upon which transient behavior becomes eternal imprint. 

This idea parallels what physics describes as a holographic boundary. Just as the Event Horizon encodes three-dimensional information onto a two-dimensional surface, the spiritual structure of creation encodes human deeds into a permanent record. Nothing evaporates. It transforms and becomes embedded in a deeper layer of existence. 

Rabbi Akiva adds another powerful phrase: “The ledger is open and the hand writes.” It sounds as though some celestial scribe is documenting our lives. But the Sfas Emes reveals a radical insight: your own hand is the hand that writes. There is no angel taking notes. The action itself generates its own inscription. 

This perfectly parallels the principle of Unitarity in quantum mechanics. The universe does not deliberate about whether to record an interaction. The interaction is the recording. Every cause carries its effect forward with mathematical precision. Reality preserves its informational integrity automatically. 

Rabbi Akiva continues: “A net is spread over all the living.” This is not a threat. It is a description of interconnectedness. Actions reverberate. Consequences propagate. The system feeds back. In physics, we encounter a striking analogue in Quantum Entanglement, where particles remain correlated across vast distances. A change in one location influences another instantly within the system’s structure. 

The Torah’s “Net” describes a moral entanglement built into creation. Tug on one strand, and the vibration travels across the whole web. Measure for measure is not vengeance—it is structural cause and effect. The moral and the physical share the same architecture. 

In this lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari synthesizes Pirkei Avot, Hasidic masters, and foundational principles of quantum physics to show that human action is not peripheral to the universe—it is central. You are not merely living inside reality; you are participating in its unfolding. The Observer Effect is not just physics. It is a metaphor for moral agency embedded in existence. 

If every deed automatically writes itself into the spiritual fabric of creation, then nothing you do is trivial. The smallest act of integrity stabilizes worlds. The smallest act of harm sends ripples across the net. The ledger is open not because we are being policed—but because we are being empowered. 

--- IN THIS VIDEO ---

Why the Book represents a permanent dimension of reality, not divine memory 

How your own actions act as the “hand” writing on the fabric of existence 

#QuantumObserver #TorahAndScience #PirkeiAvot #ObserverEffect #JewishPhilosophy #Unitarity #QuantumEntanglement #HasidicThought #RavEliyahuBari #SpiritualResponsibility

snippet.title: Quantum Physics in Pirkei Avot 5/8 – Ethics of Our Fathers – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
If every action you take writes itself into the fabric of reality, where exactly is that information stored? What is the ultimate “hard drive” of the universe—and how did it come into existence? 

The Arizal, Rabbi Isaac Luria, taught that before creation there was only Or Ein Sof—the infinite, boundless light of the Creator. There was no space for independence, no room for free will. To allow a world of choice and moral responsibility to exist, a radical process occurred: Tzimtzum, a withdrawal or concealment of infinite light. This act formed a conceptual vacuum known as the Chalal, an “empty space” in which finite reality could emerge. 

But the Chalal was not truly empty. 

The Arizal offers a striking analogy. Imagine a jar filled with thick oil. When you pour the oil out, the jar appears empty—but a subtle residue clings to its walls. That residue still carries the essence and character of what once filled it. In Kabbalah, this indestructible residue is called the Reshimu—the Trace, the Impression. 

The Reshimu is not poetic symbolism. It is described as the foundational informational imprint of creation. Kabbalistic texts explain that the Reshimu consists of Otiyot—Letters. And letters are not abstract decorations. They are discrete units of structured meaning. In computational language, they function like bits and qubits, fundamental informational building blocks. The Reshimu is the encoded DNA of existence. 

Modern physics has arrived at a remarkably parallel concept. The Holographic Principle suggests that the information describing a three-dimensional region of space can be fully encoded on a two-dimensional boundary. Reality, in other words, may function like a vast projection from an informational surface. 

Lurianic Kabbalah describes an almost identical architecture. The physical universe unfolds within the Chalal, yet its structural information is embedded in the surrounding layer of the Reshimu. The boundary holds the code. The world is not self-generating; it is data-driven. 

This convergence between Torah and theoretical physics is not superficial metaphor. It points toward a shared structural intuition: information is more fundamental than matter. Just as black hole event horizons encode physical data, the Reshimu encodes spiritual and existential data. The universe is not built from randomness—it is built from structured divine information. 

And here is where it becomes personal. 

Every time you act in the physical world, you generate energy, intention, and consequence. According to Torah thought, that energy interacts with the deeper informational layer of reality. Your deeds do not float away into nothingness. They interface with the Reshimu and modify its encoded pattern. The Cosmic Hard Drive is not static; it is responsive. 

When the Sages teach that “All your deeds are written in a book,” they are describing this very mechanism. The Book is not a celestial diary. It is the dynamic informational substrate of creation itself. Writing is not symbolic—it is ontological. Actions become code. 

From the perspective of quantum theory, interactions are never lost. Information is conserved. From the perspective of Kabbalah, spiritual impact is never erased. The Reshimu ensures continuity. Together, they describe a universe whose architecture preserves every meaningful imprint. 

This transforms our understanding of responsibility. We are not merely inhabitants of a prewritten system. We are participants in its ongoing compilation. Every choice contributes to the shaping of the cosmic record. The Trace left at the dawn of creation becomes the canvas upon which human freedom paints. 

In this lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari unpacks the depth of Or Ein Sof, Tzimtzum, Chalal, and Reshimu, connecting them with contemporary discussions about digital reality, holographic encoding, and information theory. The result is a breathtaking synthesis: Torah mysticism and modern physics both describe a universe grounded in indestructible informational structure. 

If the Reshimu is the ultimate hard drive of existence, then nothing truly disappears. The question that remains is even more astonishing: if our actions are encoded permanently, what about our identity? What about the Neshama itself? Is the human soul also a form of indestructible divine code? 

In the next part of this series, we will explore the bold and transformative idea that the soul is not fragile biological output—but eternal spiritual software, designed to transcend physical hardware.

snippet.title: Quantum Physics in Pirkei Avot 6/8 – Ethics of Our Fathers – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:

If the universe never deletes information, what happens to you when your physical body shuts down? Is death an erasure—or is it a transition of data from one level of reality to another? 

In this fifth installment of The Quantum Ledger series, Rav Eliyahu Bari confronts the most personal and profound question of all: the nature of the human soul. We have already explored how physics insists that information is conserved, how black holes cannot destroy data, and how the Torah describes an Eternal Ledger that records every action. Now we turn inward. If the cosmos preserves information, what about the information that is you? 

Orthodox Jewish thought has long taught that the Neshama is eternal. But what does that actually mean? Rabbi Aryeh Kaplan—himself trained in physics before becoming one of the most lucid expositors of Kabbalah—offered a powerful analogy. The human body is hardware. It is a biological terminal, sophisticated yet temporary. The real “self”—your personality, your memories, your accumulated choices, your moral trajectory—is software. 

In modern computational language, software is not destroyed when a single device fails. If properly preserved, it can be restored, transferred, or instantiated elsewhere. Quantum information theory echoes this principle at a deeper level. Information patterns cannot simply vanish. They may transform, become encrypted, or change form—but deletion is not part of the system. 

From a Torah perspective, the ultimate “Master File” exists within Divine Knowledge. God does not remember the way humans remember. Rather, existence itself is sustained through His knowing. If every deed is written into the cosmic Book, then every identity is likewise preserved. Death is not annihilation of the self; it is the deactivation of local hardware while the core informational pattern remains intact. 

But what about thoughts? What about fleeting, silent ideas that never became speech or action? The Tanya, foundational to Chabad Hasidic philosophy, states unequivocally that no thought is ever lost. Thoughts generate spiritual letters. They create subtle imprints in the spiritual atmosphere. Nothing evaporates without trace. 

Physics presents a striking parallel in the No-Hiding Theorem. Internal states of a system cannot be completely concealed or destroyed. Even unobserved quantum states alter the total informational configuration of reality. The universe does not permit true erasure. The structure of reality is conservation-based. 

Contemporary thinkers have drawn an even deeper analogy between death and the crossing of an Event Horizon. To outside observers, a body decays. Entropy increases. Order dissolves into apparent chaos. But from the perspective of information theory, the underlying data is not destroyed. It is conserved within a different encoding framework. 

Imagine death not as deletion, but as relocation. The Neshama transitions from a localized biological system into a non-local informational state. Just as data can move from a physical hard drive into secure cloud storage, the soul shifts from embodied expression to higher-dimensional preservation. The entropy of the body does not imply the entropy of the self. 

This reframing radically alters how we view identity, accountability, and purpose. If your core self is indestructible information, then every choice you make becomes part of a permanent structure. Your growth is cumulative. Your struggles are meaningful. Your inner life matters eternally. 

In this lecture, Rav Eliyahu Bari weaves together quantum conservation, Jewish mysticism, and philosophical clarity to show that the Torah’s doctrine of the eternal soul is not mystical escapism—it is consistent with the deepest laws of informational reality. The Neshama is not fragile biological output. It is structured divine code. 

And this leads to the ultimate question: if the informational pattern of the soul is perfectly preserved, can it ever be re-embodied? Can the divine “software” be reinstalled into renewed physical “hardware”? The Torah speaks of Techiyat HaMetim—the Resurrection of the Dead—as a future reality. Could this be understood as the ultimate act of information recovery? 

In the next part of this series, we will explore the mysterious concept of the Luz bone and uncover how Jewish tradition describes resurrection not as magic—but as restoration.

snippet.title: Quantum Physics in Pirkei Avot 7/8 – Ethics of Our Fathers – Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
Watch the complete series in order:

If your soul is indestructible divine information, can it ever be restored into a physical body? Is resurrection a supernatural interruption of nature—or the ultimate expression of the universe’s informational design? 

In this sixth installment of The Quantum Ledger series, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores one of the most astonishing teachings in Jewish thought: Techiyat HaMetim, the Resurrection of the Dead. After discovering that the universe conserves information, that the Neshama is preserved as divine “software,” and that every deed is recorded in the Cosmic Ledger, we now ask the ultimate question: is there a “restore” function built into creation? 

The Midrash teaches a remarkable idea. The future resurrection will begin from a tiny, indestructible bone known as the Luz, located at the base of the spine. The Sages describe it as resistant to decay, fire, and destruction. For centuries, many understood this as a literal anatomical mystery. But deeper Torah analysis reveals something far more profound. 

The Luz represents an irreducible informational kernel—the compressed core of personal identity. Just as advanced physics describes how a massive star can collapse into an ultra-dense state where its information is preserved in extreme compression, Jewish tradition describes the Luz as the minimal unit from which the entire human form can be reconstructed. It is not merely bone; it is code. 

Modern black hole research introduces the concept of the Page Curve, which tracks how information that appears trapped within a black hole gradually re-emerges over time. Information is not erased; it is temporarily encoded in a highly complex form before being recoverable. If black holes cannot permanently delete data, then reality itself contains a built-in mechanism of restoration. 

Techiyat HaMetim can be understood as the ultimate “Page Time” of the cosmos—the moment when the full informational record of a human being is re-instantiated into embodied existence. This is not reincarnation into a generic identity. It is precise reconstruction. The same informational structure—the same personality architecture, the same moral trajectory, the same spiritual growth—is restored in high fidelity. 

But this revelation raises a profound concern. If the Resurrection reconstructs us from the exact record preserved in the Heavenly Ledger, what about our failures? What about the mistakes permanently encoded in the system? If information cannot be destroyed, are sins eternally frozen in our spiritual profile? 

Here the Torah introduces one of its most revolutionary ideas: Teshuvah. At first glance, physics seems unforgiving. The past is fixed. Causes produce effects in one direction. But Jewish tradition teaches that genuine Teshuvah—repentance motivated by love and transformation—can reconfigure the meaning of past actions. The Talmud even states that intentional sins can be transformed into merits. 

This does not imply deletion. Deleting information would contradict the very principle of conservation that underlies both physics and the Cosmic Ledger. Instead, Teshuvah operates at a higher layer. It alters context, polarity, and narrative integration. The raw data remains conserved, but its interpretive value flips. What was once a spiritual deficit becomes the catalyst for growth. 

In informational terms, Teshuvah edits metadata without violating conservation laws. The event remains in the ledger, but its spiritual charge changes. The system is not read-only. It is interactive. Human free will is granted extraordinary access—not to erase history, but to elevate it. 

This idea reframes accountability in a breathtaking way. We are neither trapped by our past nor able to pretend it never happened. We are empowered to transform it. The same “hand that writes” our deeds is authorized to rewrite their trajectory through sincere return. 



The Luz is not merely a mystical bone. It is the symbolic compression of identity. Techiyat HaMetim is not arbitrary revival. It is the ultimate download from the Divine Cloud. Teshuvah is not emotional relief. It is code-level editing within the Cosmic Ledger. 

In the final video of this series, we will bring together all these ideas—quantum conservation, the Reshimu, the Neshama, the Heavenly Book, and Teshuvah—and discover why these concepts are not abstract philosophy, but a powerful call to live with awareness, courage, and responsibility every single day.

After exploring black holes, quantum mechanics, Kabbalah, the Reshimu, the Neshama, the Luz, and Techiyat HaMetim, we now arrive at the ultimate question: What does this mean for how you live today? 

In this final installment of The Quantum Ledger series, Rav Eliyahu Bari brings the entire journey together into one breathtaking conclusion. We began with physics—discovering that information is never destroyed. We saw how the Black Hole Information Paradox forced scientists to confront the terrifying possibility of cosmic forgetfulness, only to conclude that the universe preserves every bit of data. We then turned to Torah, uncovering that our Sages described a “Book of Remembrance” thousands of years ago, teaching that all deeds are written and never erased. 

When these two worlds converge, a stunning symmetry appears. 

The Kabbalistic Reshimu functions as the boundary information layer of existence. The “Hand that Writes” mirrors the automatic conservation laws of quantum mechanics. The Luz represents the compressed core of identity. Techiyat HaMetim emerges as the ultimate restoration of preserved data. What once sounded mystical now reads like a profound description of informational architecture. 

This is not an attempt to reduce Torah to physics, nor to reduce physics to religion. It is the recognition that both disciplines are describing the same deep structure from different languages. One speaks in equations; the other in sacred metaphor. Together, they reveal a universe that is not random, not forgetful, and not indifferent. 

And here lies the ethical revolution. 

In a pre-quantum worldview, one might imagine that darkness hides actions. Close the door, turn off the lights, and the moment disappears. But in a universe governed by information conservation, there is no true deletion. The darkness itself records. Every interaction modifies the system. Every choice alters the code. 

This idea could sound frightening—but it is profoundly empowering. The “Eye that Sees” is not cosmic surveillance; it is existential validation. To be observed is to be sustained. To act is to inscribe. Existence itself is participation in a living text. 

Modern Torah thinkers have pointed out that the word “universe” can be understood as a single unfolding expression—a unified narrative. The laws of physics are its grammar and syntax. The Torah provides its semantics and meaning. Without syntax, language collapses into chaos. Without meaning, grammar becomes empty. Together, they form a coherent story. 

The realization that nothing is forgotten is both demand and consolation. It demands responsibility because every action carries eternal consequence. But it consoles because nothing meaningful is ever wasted. No silent prayer vanishes. No hidden act of integrity evaporates. No struggle toward goodness is lost in the void. 

You are not a temporary biochemical accident destined for oblivion. You are an information-generating being embedded in a conservation-based cosmos. Your life writes data that survives the death of stars. The cosmic ledger does not merely judge—it preserves. 

The Baal Shem Tov taught that memory is the root of redemption. To remember who we are—beings created in the image of the Divine, capable of shaping eternal impact—is to reclaim dignity and direction. When we understand that our actions are permanently inscribed into the fabric of reality, we begin to live differently. We act with intention. We speak with awareness. We think with purpose. 

This is the ultimate readout of the Quantum Ledger: your life matters forever. 

Every mitzvah, every moment of growth, every ethical decision is a line of code that will one day be revealed in its full brilliance. The final “readout” at the end of days is not a surprise audit; it is the unveiling of the story you have been writing all along. 

If the universe remembers, then your choices echo beyond time. If the soul is preserved, then growth is cumulative. If Teshuvah can transform the past, then no chapter is beyond redemption. 

The ledger is open. The hand writes. And the story is yours.

snippet.description:

🔥 COULD YOU CHEAT GOD'S MANNA SYSTEM? 🔥

For 40 years in the wilderness, our ancestors lived on manna—a food that defied all known laws of nature, economics, and physics. Each person was allocated exactly one omer per day. But here's an intriguing question: What if someone tried to cheat the system? Could you eat manna right there in the field while gathering, then still bring home your full omer?

In this class, we deeply investigate this question through the lens of the great Torah commentators.

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS:
00:00 - Introduction: A Puzzle in the Wilderness
05:30 - How the Miracle Worked: The Equalization
12:15 - Rashi: The Miracle of Volume
16:40 - Malbim: The Satiety Factor
21:00 - Netziv: The Personalized Omer
25:20 - Halachic Analysis: Is This Stealing?
32:45 - The Biology of Manna: Why You Physically Couldn't Cheat
38:10 - Gemara Yoma 75a: Food With No Waste
43:30 - The Wicked vs. The Righteous
48:00 - "Nothing Over" - The Final Seal
53:15 - The Shabbat Exception Proves the Rule
57:40 - Conclusion: Why the Loophole Is Impossible

📚 FOUR TYPES OF IMPOSSIBILITY:

1️⃣ METAPHYSICAL: The omer measured your soul's capacity for that day. (Rashi, Malbim) The miracle was retroactive—stomach content + basket content = always exactly 1 omer.

2️⃣ BIOLOGICAL: Manna was "lechem abirim"—absorbed completely, NO WASTE (Yoma 75a). Your body was like a vessel; once full with one omer, no more could fit.

3️⃣ LEGAL/SPIRITUAL: Not "poel" (worker's lunch)—this was bread from heaven with specific divine terms. (Brisker Rav) The omer defined manna's very existence for you. Eating unmeasured = "gezel" (theft) from Hashem—you'd get calories but miss spiritual nourishment.

4️⃣ LOGISTICAL: For the faithless, manna was hard coriander seeds requiring grinding, pounding, boiling. The sun heats up and manna melts (Exodus 16:21). The righteous found ready-to-eat bread at their doorstep.

🎯 KEY CONCEPTS:
• Bitachon (absolute trust in Divine providence)
• The equalization miracle
• Lechem min hashamayim (bread from heaven)
• Divine justice and economics
• Spiritual food vs. physical food
• Da'at (knowledge) as a metaphor for manna

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS TODAY:
Manna teaches us that Hashem provides exactly what we need, when we need it, in the way we need it. Our job is to trust the system, not try to outsmart it. In the face of Divine Providence, there are no loopholes.

05:30 - How the Miracle Worked: The Equalization

📚 FOUR TYPES OF IMPOSSIBILITY:

1️⃣ METAPHYSICAL: The omer measured your soul's capacity for that day. (Rashi, Malbim) The miracle was retroactive—stomach content + basket content = always exactly 1 omer.

2️⃣ BIOLOGICAL: Manna was "lechem abirim"—absorbed completely, NO WASTE (Yoma 75a). Your body was like a vessel; once full with one omer, no more could fit.

3️⃣ LEGAL/SPIRITUAL: Not "poel" (worker's lunch)—this was bread from heaven with specific divine terms. (Brisker Rav) The omer defined manna's very existence for you. Eating unmeasured = "gezel" (theft) from Hashem—you'd get calories but miss spiritual nourishment.

4️⃣ LOGISTICAL: For the faithless, manna was hard coriander seeds requiring grinding, pounding, boiling. The sun heats up and manna melts (Exodus 16:21). The righteous found ready-to-eat bread at their doorstep.

🎯 KEY CONCEPTS:
• Bitachon (absolute trust in Divine providence)
• The equalization miracle
• Lechem min hashamayim (bread from heaven)
• Divine justice and economics
• Spiritual food vs. physical food
• Da'at (knowledge) as a metaphor for manna

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS TODAY:
Manna teaches us that Hashem provides exactly what we need, when we need it, in the way we need it. Our job is to trust the system, not try to outsmart it. In the face of Divine Providence, there are no loopholes.

snippet.title: Shemini Atzeret: The Joy of Torah | Arizal on Sukkot 5 | Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
​Why does the journey from Rosh Hashanah through Sukkot culminate in Shemini Atzeret? Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the Arizal’s teaching on spiritual union, the joy of Torah, and light becoming life-giving influence. 
 
This is Video 5 of 5, the finale of The Arizal on Sukkot: “Shemini Atzeret: What Was the Entire Journey For?” We bring together the themes of separation, rebuilding, judgment, kindness, and the two seals. Their purpose is more than avoiding an unfavorable judgment. The sequence prepares for the fullness of a relationship with Hashem and for a joy that can continue after the festival. 
 
The principal source is the ninth discourse on Sukkot in Sha’ar HaKavanot, transmitted by Rabbi Chaim Vital. The class distinguishes building a spiritual configuration from preparing for union and from union itself. We then consider the Talmud’s image of a small meal with the king, the mention of rain in Musaf, and the Arizal’s explanation of Simchat Torah. 
 
BUILDING AND UNION 
Rachel’s development unfolds through nesirah, standing face to face, receiving chasadim, and receiving two seals. Yet preparing the capacity for a relationship and realizing it are distinct stages. The particular union of Ze’ir Anpin and Rachel discussed here belongs to Musaf on Shemini Atzeret. We do not collapse the different processes of the month into one event. The term zivug describes spiritual union between transmitting and receiving principles, not a physical action. 
 
WHAT WAS THE PREPARATION FOR? 
As an analogy, tuning an instrument and playing music are connected but different. The preparation has a purpose beyond itself. Likewise, the class asks what happens when the relationship prepared through the festivals becomes a reality. This everyday illustration helps frame the question; it does not replace the Arizal’s technical explanation. 
 
A SMALL MEAL WITH THE KING 
The Talmud in Sukkah 55b connects the seventy bulls of Sukkot with the seventy nations and the single bull of Shemini Atzeret with Israel. Its parable describes a king who, after a great feast, wants a small meal with his friend. This independent Talmudic teaching helps us hear the theme of particular closeness at the festival’s conclusion. The lesson keeps that parable distinct from the Arizal’s account while considering how both direct attention to the relationship itself. 
 
WHY GEVUROT REMAIN 
The ninth discourse describes new gevurot received in the union, distinct from those involved in preparing the vessel on Hoshana Rabbah. They are associated with a more sweetened state. Gevurah is not simply another word for evil: strength, definition, and the ability to form a vessel have a place within a corrected relationship. For our own conduct, closeness can coexist with responsibility, and forgiveness need not erase the weight of a promise. These are ethical reflections on the theme. 
 
FROM LIGHT TO WATER 
At Musaf on Shemini Atzeret, we begin mentioning rain in prayer. The class distinguishes this mention from the seasonal request for rain, whose starting date is not the same everywhere. Drawing on the Zohar, Sha’ar HaKavanot presents “or, mayim, rakia”: light, water, firmament. These describe stages of influence and formation in the source, not a physical theory of weather. The image invites us to ask how the elevated experience of the festivals can nourish ordinary life. 
 
WHY THE JOY OF TORAH? 
The Arizal explains Simchat Torah through Ze’ir Anpin, called Torah, and the joy of his union with Rachel. This adds a particular Kabbalistic meaning to the joy of completing and renewing the Torah-reading cycle. In Israel, Simchat Torah is celebrated on Shemini Atzeret; in the Diaspora, on the following day. The lesson preserves this distinction while exploring their shared place at the culmination of the festivals. 
 
THE ARIZAL’S OWN JOY 
Rabbi Chaim Vital describes his teacher singing and dancing with the Torah scroll and joining circuits in different synagogues after Yom Tov ended. He also notes that he was not present for the daytime circuits. We retain the limits of that testimony. The account shows how profound study found expression in the joy of a mitzvah, without adding details the student did not witness. 
 
AFTER THE FESTIVAL 
What will remain when the festive setting is gone? Choose one continuation: regular Torah study, an act of help, or gratitude before making a demand. Revisit the series from the embrace after forgiveness through the sukkah, four species, and Hoshana Rabbah. The final question is where this renewed relationship will bear fruit in daily life. 
 
SOURCES 
Rabbi Chaim Vital, Sha’ar HaKavanot, Derushei Chag HaSukkot, discourse 9 and the testimony in discourses 1–2; Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 55b; Zohar II, 167a, cited in discourse 9; Vayikra 23:36.

snippet.title: Hoshana Rabbah: Arizal - The Second Seal and Five Branches | Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
​Wasn’t the judgment already sealed on Yom Kippur? Rav Eliyahu Bari explores Hoshana Rabbah through the Arizal’s teaching on the second seal, seven circuits, and five willow branches. 
 
This is Video 4 of the five-part series The Arizal on Sukkot: “Hoshana Rabbah: The Second Seal and Five Branches.” After the sukkah’s surrounding light and the movements of the four species, we reach the final day of Sukkot. Festive joy continues, yet judgment and sealing return to the foreground. What still needs to be completed, and how does this day prepare for Shemini Atzeret? 
 
Drawing on Sha’ar HaKavanot as transmitted by Rabbi Chaim Vital, especially the sixth and eighth discourses on Sukkot, the class distinguishes the inner seal from the outer seal, the handing over of judgments from permission to carry them out, and receiving kindness from becoming ready to respond. These connected stages give the day a meaning deeper than a repeated deadline. 
 
A SEAL WITHIN A SEAL 
At Ne’ilah on Yom Kippur, Rachel receives five gevurot from Imma, and the principal inner seal is formed in Nukva’s Yesod. The seal protects what has been received from attachment by external forces. On the night of Hoshana Rabbah, a second, outer seal is formed in Nukva’s Malchut, the concluding aspect of her Yesod. It also originates from Imma. The second seal builds on the first; it does not mean that the work of Yom Kippur failed or disappeared. 
 
WHAT DOES A SEAL PROTECT? 
In this account, sealing is more than confirming a judicial decision. It concerns a protected spiritual vessel and the proper preservation of influence. The language of external forces describes the possibility of drawing nourishment from an unrectified state of holiness. It is not a description of physical beings standing beside a sukkah. The class keeps these spiritual relationships distinct from the everyday examples used to make the subject approachable. 
 
WHY READ DEVARIM AT NIGHT? 
The Arizal connects the reading of Devarim, also called Mishneh Torah, with the repeated, secondary seal. Torah’s light receives a further reflection at the concluding level. The nighttime order describes reading the entire book through Vezot HaBerachah during the first half of the night. We consider how this practice belongs to the wider process of sealing, and then ask a practical question of our own: how can returning to a commitment help establish it firmly in daily life? 
 
JUDGMENT AND THE POSSIBILITY OF RETURN 
Sha’ar HaKavanot distinguishes the sealing and handing over associated with Hoshana Rabbah from permission to execute judgments on Shemini Atzeret. During Hoshana Rabbah, teshuvah remains possible. The source itself emphasizes genuine return and correcting one’s actions. This annual sequence does not mean repentance becomes useless afterward: Rambam teaches that teshuvah and calling out to Hashem are always beneficial. A ritual does not replace repentance or guarantee a particular outcome. 
 
WHY SEVEN CIRCUITS? 
Hoshana Rabbah completes the seven-day revelation of chasadim in Malchut. Rabbi Chaim Vital offers an explanation of the seven circuits as expressing the gathering of preceding influences into the final level. He identifies this as his own understanding before separately recording what he heard from his teacher. The lesson preserves that distinction between the Arizal’s teaching and his student’s explanation. Accurate attribution helps us study the source with care. 
 
FIVE WILLOW BRANCHES AND FIVE GEVUROT 
After the circuits, five separate aravah branches are taken. They are associated with five gevurot and preparing a vessel for mayin nukvin, the ascending awakening of the receiving side, ahead of the union of Shemini Atzeret. The five strikes against the ground are explained through drawing the gevurot down to Malchut and weakening the severity of judgment. The branches do not simply “beat sins away.” Their role belongs to the spiritual preparation unfolding throughout the festivals. 
 
PRESERVE AND RESPOND 
The receiving side must become ready to participate, rather than remain passive. As a practical reflection, ask: what will protect the good I have already accepted? A fixed time for study, a pause before a sharp reply, or a specific act of generosity can help preserve the fruit of inspiration. These examples accompany the source’s technical account; they do not replace its kavanot. 
 
NEXT IN THE SERIES 
Video 5: “Shemini Atzeret: What Was the Entire Journey For?” We turn to the realization of the relationship prepared throughout Tishrei and its connection with the joy of Torah. 
 
SOURCES 
Rabbi Chaim Vital, Sha’ar HaKavanot, Derushei Chag HaSukkot, discourses 6 and 8, with the nighttime order in discourse 2; Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot Teshuvah 2:6. 
 
Subscribe for the concluding lesson, share this class, and comment: what concrete step will help you preserve a good commitment after the festival?

snippet.title: Sukkot: Why Do We Shake the Lulav? The Arizal's Secret | 3/5 | Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
​Why do we move the lulav after taking the four species? Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the Arizal’s teaching on Sukkot, the lulav and etrog, and how inner light is received and transmitted. 
 
This is Video 3 of the five-part series The Arizal on Sukkot: “The Four Species: How Inner Light Arrives.” In the previous lesson, we entered the sukkah as a space of surrounding kindness. Now we turn to the movements of the four species and the chasadim of Ze’ir Anpin, whose illumination reaches Nukva. The familiar action contains a precise account of drawing light from its root and bringing it toward the receiving level. 
 
Based primarily on the fifth discourse on Sukkot in Sha’ar HaKavanot, transmitted by Rabbi Chaim Vital, this class asks why four species contain seven principal components, what Yesod gathers, and why extending the lulav outward is followed by bringing it back. We also distinguish the movements from the Hoshanot circuits, so that inner and surrounding influences are not confused. 
 
FOUR SPECIES, SEVEN COMPONENTS 
Three myrtle branches, two willow branches, one lulav, and one etrog make seven individual components. In this discourse, the three hadassim correspond to Chesed, Gevurah, and Tiferet; the two aravot to Netzach and Hod; and the lulav to Yesod. The etrog represents Malchut within Ze’ir Anpin himself, the concluding aspect of his Yesod. The Arizal also clarifies that the plants indicate the chasadim spreading within these attributes, rather than simply the sefirot considered on their own. 
 
WHY THE ETROG’S PLACE MATTERS 
The lesson follows the source’s specific explanation. Here the etrog is not identified with the separate receiving configuration of Rachel. The whole set belongs to the transmitting side of Ze’ir Anpin. Keeping that distinction allows us to understand both the unity within the source of transmission and its relationship to Nukva, who receives the influence. A general statement about unity cannot replace the details of this account. 
 
WHAT YESOD GATHERS 
Yesod gathers the influences of the preceding attributes and serves to transmit them. The lulav is associated with Yesod and with the image of the spinal column. Bringing the lulav and etrog together is therefore integral to the teaching. As an everyday analogy, good intentions, patience, and understanding need to become coordinated action before another person actually receives help. This example illustrates the question of transmission; it does not define the Kabbalistic meaning of Yesod. 
 
EXTENDING AND RETURNING 
Extending the lulav awakens an ascent toward the root of the chasadim in the Da’at of Ze’ir Anpin, from which illumination is received. Returning it draws that illumination toward Nukva. Bringing it back toward the chest relates to the place where Rachel’s configuration begins in the state described. Physical direction is not a literal map of spiritual worlds: the outward gesture can express turning toward a higher root. The action joins receiving from the source with passing on what has been received. 
 
SIX DIRECTIONS 
Sha’ar HaKavanot gives the order south, north, east, up, down, and west, corresponding to Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, and Yesod. Each involves three extensions and returns, connected in the text with the inclusion of three mochin. West concludes the sequence through Yesod’s gathering role. The class explains this source’s order while recognizing that communities differ in practice. It is a study of the teaching, not an instruction to replace your established custom. 
 
MOVEMENTS AND CIRCUITS 
The lulav’s movements are associated with inner chasadim; the circuits with surrounding chasadim from Ze’ir Anpin. This surrounding influence is distinct from the surrounding chasadim of Imma discussed in relation to the sukkah. The class also follows the unfolding of the festival toward Malchut on Hoshana Rabbah. Alongside the mystical explanation, we recall the Mishnah’s account of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai instituting taking the lulav for seven days outside the Temple in remembrance of the Temple. 
 
FROM INSPIRATION TO ACTION 
What do I bring home from a moment of inspiration? A class or prayer can move me, yet another person still needs my time, attention, or help. The practical question is how kindness reaches someone through a concrete deed. These ethical reflections accompany the source; they do not replace its kavanot. 
 
NEXT IN THE SERIES 
Video 4 turns to Hoshana Rabbah: the second seal, seven circuits, and five willow branches. Why does a festival associated with kindness conclude with renewed attention to judgment and sealing? 
 
SOURCES 
Rabbi Chaim Vital, Sha’ar HaKavanot, Derushei Chag HaSukkot, especially discourse 5, with related material in discourses 1–2; Mishnah Sukkah 3:12.

snippet.title: The Sukkah: Light We Live Within | Arizal on Sukkot 2 | Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
​​Why do we enter a sukkah with our whole body? Rav Eliyahu Bari explores the Arizal’s teaching on Sukkot, surrounding light, and the walls of the sukkah as an embrace of Divine kindness. 
 
This is Video 2 of the five-part series The Arizal on Sukkot: “The Sukkah: Light We Live Within.” After the first lesson’s journey from judgment and forgiveness toward renewed closeness, we turn to the space in which that closeness becomes the setting of daily life. We eat, sit, speak, and welcome guests inside the sukkah. What does it mean to enter a mitzvah rather than perform it with only one part of ourselves? 
 
The class draws on Sha’ar HaKavanot, the teachings of the Arizal transmitted by Rabbi Chaim Vital, especially the third and fourth discourses on Sukkot. We explore the distinction between inner light and surrounding light, the shelter associated with Imma, the seven Clouds of Glory, and the image of the right arm embracing. Alongside the technical teaching, everyday examples help us consider how kindness can shape the atmosphere of a home and a festival table. 
 
INNER LIGHT AND SURROUNDING LIGHT 
Inner light is received within a vessel; surrounding light encompasses it. The Hebrew term or makif does not mean a visible glow around a person or a building. It describes a spiritual relationship between light and its recipient. Nor is surrounding light simply something unwanted or left over. It remains connected to the vessel, even when it cannot yet be received inwardly. The sukkah gives this distinction a central place in our understanding of Sukkot. We can enter the mitzvah before we can fully explain everything it contains. 
 
WHY THE FESTIVAL IS CALLED SUKKOT 
The Arizal connects the sukkah with the surrounding chasadim, the influences of kindness associated with Imma. Imma is the higher configuration associated with Binah, portrayed as sheltering her children, Ze’ir Anpin and Nukva. These terms describe relationships within the teaching. The class distinguishes the sukkah in relation to each recipient and to both together, instead of treating every reference as one interchangeable label. The question is who gives shelter, who receives it, and how closeness is renewed. 
 
SEVEN CLOUDS, SEVEN DAYS 
The Torah commands us to dwell in sukkot in remembrance of the Exodus. In the Arizal’s account, the Clouds of Glory are connected with surrounding kindness. Seven clouds correspond to seven surrounding chasadim and the seven lower sefirot of Nukva. Their unfolding across the festival proceeds from Chesed toward Malchut. This is a different order from the inner chasadim discussed in Video 1. Keeping the two processes distinct helps us see why each day matters, even when the same walls and table remain before us. 
 
THE WALLS AS AN EMBRACE 
The image of the right arm embracing is rooted in Shir HaShirim, the Song of Songs. The Arizal relates the sukkah’s two full walls and a third wall of the required minimum size to the two longer sections of an arm and the hand. The architectural form becomes an image of shelter and closeness, connected with the face-to-face relationship of Ze’ir Anpin and Nukva. This discussion explains the mystical meaning of the walls; it is not a complete guide to the practical laws of building a kosher sukkah. 
 
THE SHADE OF FAITH AND THE OPEN TABLE 
The Zohar calls the sukkah the shade of faith and speaks of the ushpizin, the exalted guests. It also insists that festive hospitality include those in need. The spiritual guests cannot become an excuse to overlook actual people. We consider what it means to share food, make room for someone who is alone, and welcome a guest with dignity. The practical reflections illustrate how the teaching can inform our conduct; they are distinguished from the Arizal’s technical descriptions and intentions. 
 
A QUESTION TO TAKE INTO THE SUKKAH 
If I understand myself as held within kindness, how might I speak differently? Could I soften a demand for a perfect holiday, listen more patiently, or notice someone who has no place at the table? A warm welcome is more than an impressive setting. The lesson invites us to connect the encompassing space of the mitzvah with the quality of the relationships we bring into it. 
 
SERIES CONTINUITY 
Previous lesson: why Sukkot follows Yom Kippur and how forgiveness opens toward an embrace. Next, Video 3: “Four Species: How Inner Light Arrives.” We will turn from the sukkah’s surrounding light to the four species, the lulav, and their movements. The full series continues through Hoshana Rabbah and Shemini Atzeret. 
 
SOURCES 
Rabbi Chaim Vital, Sha’ar HaKavanot, Derushei Chag HaSukkot, discourses 3–4; Zohar III, Emor, 103b–104a; Vayikra (Leviticus) 23:42–43; Shir HaShirim 2:6 and 8:3.

snippet.title: The Arizal on Sukkot: Why Forgiveness Is Only the Beginning | Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
​Why does Sukkot follow Yom Kippur? Discover the Arizal’s teaching on the journey from judgment and forgiveness to the embrace of Divine kindness. 
 
In Video 1 of The Arizal on Sukkot, Rav Eliyahu Bari explores why the spiritual process does not end with Ne’ilah. After fasting and confession, we enter a sukkah, share festive meals, and rejoice. In the Arizal’s account, these are connected stages in the renewal of closeness to Hashem. 
 
Drawing on Sha’ar HaKavanot, as transmitted by Rabbi Chaim Vital, this class explores the left-arm and right-arm embraces described through Shir HaShirim; gevurot and their sweetening through chasadim; and the spiritual meaning of the four days between Yom Kippur and Sukkot. 
 
Why do the inner chasadim enter from below upward? What is a roshem—a lasting spiritual trace? How can each stage prepare the way for the next? We also introduce the distinction between inner and surrounding light and the sukkah’s connection to the surrounding chasadim of Imma. 
 
The class includes a brief introduction to Ze’ir Anpin, Nukva, and the transition from “back to back” to “face to face,” so you can join even if you missed the earlier Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur classes. Practical examples illustrate the teaching while remaining distinct from the Arizal’s technical account. 
 
THE JOURNEY DOES NOT END WITH FORGIVENESS 
Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur prepare a renewed relationship, but preparation is not the same as its completion. The Arizal places the particular union of Ze’ir Anpin and Rachel discussed here on Shemini Atzeret. Sukkot therefore has its own necessary role: the movement toward closeness continues through kindness, joy, and the experience of dwelling within a mitzvah. 
 
THE LEFT ARM AND THE RIGHT ARM 
“His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand embraces me.” The verse provides the central image for this class. The left side corresponds to gevurah: discernment, boundaries, and judgment. Yet even the left arm belongs to an embrace. The lesson asks how judgment can participate in restoring closeness, and why chasadim—the influences of kindness—are needed for the next stage. 
 
FOUR DAYS OF PREPARATION, ONE CONTINUING PROCESS 
The eleventh through fourteenth of Tishrei are more than a practical interval for building a sukkah and preparing for the festival. In the sequence examined in this class, inner chasadim from Imma enter Nukva’s Hod, Netzach, Tiferet, and Gevurah, with Chesed following on the first day of Sukkot. We also note the earlier collective illuminations in Malchut and Yesod, so this gradual process is not presented as beginning from nothing. 
 
WHY THE SMALLER STEPS COME FIRST 
Rabbi Chaim Vital explains that the gevurot have become strong during the preceding days. The successive entry of chasadim prepares the spiritual structure for a fuller influence. Each stage leaves a roshem, a trace that continues to matter when the next stage arrives. This gives the class its practical question: can we recognize the value of a step that has begun a repair without yet completing it? 
 
FROM SPIRITUAL LANGUAGE TO DAILY LIFE 
An embrace is a way of describing spiritual relationship, not a physical image of Hashem. Likewise, inner and surrounding light describe the relationship of spiritual influence to a vessel. Everyday examples help us approach these ideas: pausing before a harsh response, expressing gratitude, or helping prepare for the festival with greater patience. These applications are illustrations for our own inner work, not quotations from the Arizal. 
 
LEARNING TO LIVE WITHIN RENEWED CLOSENESS 
Someone may hear that he has been forgiven and still feel as if he is only being tolerated. Sukkot invites us to consider what comes next: entering, remaining, sharing a table, and allowing joy to become part of a renewed relationship. Joy does not erase the responsibility of Yom Kippur. The lesson explores how repentance can lead into a life with more gratitude, generosity, and peaceful closeness. 
 
The sukkah, the lulav, and the festival’s joy are introduced here as parts of one unfolding journey. This opening lesson establishes the framework for the series, while the following classes develop the sukkah’s walls, the four species, Hoshana Rabbah, and Shemini Atzeret in greater detail. 
 
The question to take into the festival: what small trace of repair can I leave today? 
 
This is Part 1 of a five-video series continuing through Sukkot, Hoshana Rabbah, and Shemini Atzeret. Next: The Sukkah—Light We Live Within. 
 
Principal source: Sha’ar HaKavanot, Derushei Chag HaSukkot, especially discourse 3; with related passages in discourses 1–2, 4–5, and 9. Biblical image: Shir HaShirim 2:6 and 8:3.

snippet.title: Arizal - Yom Kippur 3/3: Kapparah, Neilah & the Road to Sukkot | Rav Eliyahu Bari
snippet.description:
What does kapparah really mean — and why does Yom Kippur end with Neilah, Shema Yisrael, and then lead immediately toward Sukkot? 
 
In the final part of Rav Eliyahu Bari’s three-video Yom Kippur series according to the Arizal, the entire process becomes personal. After the building of Malchut, the ascent toward Imma, the sweetening of the Dinim, and the Avodah of the Kohen Gadol, we return to the word that defines the day for most people: kapparah. 
 
Kapparah is usually translated as atonement or forgiveness. But if a sin damages a spiritual relationship, then forgiveness cannot mean only that a heavenly record has been erased or that a legal case has been closed. The relationship itself has to be repaired. 
 
This is where Teshuvah, kapparah, and the building of Malchut come together. The person returns. The Dinim are sweetened. The damaged structure is restored. The lower realm again becomes capable of receiving from the higher. Yom Kippur offers not merely cancellation of punishment, but the possibility of genuine tikkun. 
 
Then we arrive at Neilah. The usual image is that the gates are closing and we must enter before it is too late. The inner tradition gives us another powerful perspective: perhaps the gates are not only closing in front of us — perhaps they are closing behind us. 
 
All day we have been moving inward and upward. Later Chassidic teaching especially associates the climax with Yechidah, from yachid — the unique, essential point of the soul. At that level, the relationship with Hashem is deeper than intellectual understanding, emotional inspiration, or even a person’s present spiritual performance. It is the essential belonging of the soul to its Source. 
 
This changes the question of Neilah. It is no longer only, “Will Hashem forgive me?” It becomes, “Who am I really?” And the answer is that at the deepest point, the bond was never completely lost. 
 
We then examine why Yom Kippur ends with Shema Yisrael, Baruch Shem, and seven declarations of Hashem Hu HaElokim. After the complex language of Sefirot, Partzufim, Mochin, Gevurot, and spiritual ascent, everything resolves into one word: Echad — One. From separation to unity. From damage to tikkun. From distance to closeness. 
 
But the series does not end there, because Tishrei does not end at Neilah. 
 
Only a few days later, the Torah tells us to enter the sukkah. Yom Kippur moved upward: away from normal physical life and toward the inner root. Sukkot begins the next movement. What was attained above must now surround us and enter ordinary physical existence. We eat and drink again — but inside the sukkah. The theme of or makif, encompassing light, becomes central. 
 
This final episode therefore closes the Yom Kippur series while deliberately opening the next chapter: Sukkot, the Four Species, Hoshana Rabbah, Shemini Atzeret, and Simchat Torah. 
 
Rosh Hashanah began the rebuilding. Yom Kippur brought ascent, sweetening, and inner return. Sukkot will show how that light begins to surround life itself. 
 
Continue the High Holidays journey with Rav Eliyahu Bari in the next series on Sukkot according to the Arizal.
